questions.title: Find the Head of a Live Blocking Chain
questions.prompt: Users are reporting the application is frozen. You suspect blocking, not an outage. Write the T-SQL you'd run right now against the live server to find the head blocker — the session that isn't waiting on anyone else but is blocking everyone downstream — and explain what you'd do with the session ID once you have it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests joined to sys.dm_exec_sessions, filtering for sessions that have a non-zero blocking_session_id to see everyone currently blocked, then specifically look for the blocking_session_id value that does not itself appear as a session_id with its own non-zero blocking_session_id — that session is the head blocker, the one actually holding the lock everyone else is waiting on. Once I have it, I'd pull its current or last statement via sys.dm_exec_sql_text and check open_tran_count and last_request_start_time to understand what it's actually doing and how long it's been doing it, rather than acting blind. Only if it's clearly stuck or abnormally long-running would I consider KILLing the session, understanding that the kill itself rolls back its transaction and can take as long or longer than letting it finish. The real fix afterward is to find out why that session held locks so long — a missing index causing a slow scan while holding a write lock, or application code that doesn't commit promptly — because KILL is an emergency release valve, not a repeatable procedure.
questions.example:
SELECT 
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    t.text AS running_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.session_id IN (
    SELECT blocking_session_id FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0
)
AND r.blocking_session_id = 0;  -- the head blocker: blocking others, blocked by no one
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'the app is frozen,' my first move is never to panic and start killing sessions — it's to find out if this is actually blocking, and if so, where it starts. I'd run a query against dm_exec_requests joined to dm_exec_sessions, filtering for anyone currently blocked, and then specifically look for the one session that's blocking others but isn't itself waiting on anyone — that's my head blocker. Before I touch it, I want to know what it's actually running and how long it's been running it, because killing it rolls back its transaction, and that rollback can take just as long as letting it finish. Once things are stable again, the real work starts: finding out why that session held locks that long in the first place, because if I don't fix that, I'm back here again next week.
commonMistakes: Immediately KILLs a session without identifying the actual head blocker first
Confuses a long-running query with a blocking chain — not every slow query is blocking others
Doesn't capture what the head blocker's own transaction was doing before acting
Treats sp_who2 output alone as sufficient without the actual SQL text or wait info
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the head-blocker query pattern using DMVs
Explains the difference between being blocked and being the source of blocking
Describes a safe escalation path (investigate before KILL)
Connects the fix back to root cause (missing index, long transaction, app behavior)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working query identifying the head blocker
Explains the DMV logic clearly
Describes a safe, sensible escalation/response procedure
Connects to durable root-cause fix, not just killing sessions

questions.title: Replace a Row-by-Row Price Update With a Set-Based Rewrite
questions.prompt: A nightly job uses a cursor to apply a different percentage increase to ListPrice per product category, reading category-specific rates from a rates table. It takes 40 minutes against 2 million products. Rewrite it as a single set-based statement.
questions.modelAnswer: The cursor's cost comes from processing one row at a time — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, each with its own overhead, multiplied by two million. SQL Server's storage engine is built to process sets of rows efficiently, so the fix is to express the same logic as a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, letting the engine apply the whole operation at once instead of looping. I'd use ISNULL to handle any product whose subcategory has no matching rate, so it's left unchanged rather than silently zeroed out by a NULL multiplication. I'd check that the join column is indexed before declaring victory, and only consider batching the update (e.g., with TOP(n) in a loop) if the single statement itself causes problematic lock duration or transaction log growth at this volume — I wouldn't reach for batching as the first move.
questions.professionalAnswer: Forty minutes for two million rows is a huge tell that something's being processed one row at a time, and sure enough, that's exactly what the cursor is doing — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, over and over. My rewrite is a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, because that lets the storage engine do what it's actually built for, which is operating on a whole set at once instead of looping. The one detail I wouldn't skip is handling products whose subcategory has no matching rate — I use a LEFT JOIN with ISNULL so those rows just stay unchanged instead of silently getting multiplied by a NULL. And I'd check the join column has an index before I call this done, because a 40-minute cursor sometimes hides a missing index underneath it too.
commonMistakes: Keeps per-row logic inside a WHILE loop over a temp table, which is just a hand-rolled cursor
Forgets to handle categories with no matching rate row (NULL rate silently zeroing the increase)
Doesn't check whether the join column is indexed before declaring victory
Jumps to batching/chunking as the first solution instead of trying the plain set-based statement first
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the cursor as the core bottleneck, not server hardware
Produces a correct, equivalent set-based UPDATE...FROM
Handles the no-matching-rate case correctly (ISNULL or join behavior)
Considers indexing and batching only as secondary, scale-driven refinements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses cursor overhead as root cause
Produces a correct, working set-based rewrite
Handles edge cases (no matching rate) correctly
Discusses sensible secondary considerations (indexing, batching) without over-engineering

questions.title: Write a tiered customer-value measure with VAR and ALLEXCEPT
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure against FactInternetSales/DimCustomer that classifies every customer into 'Platinum' (>= $50,000 lifetime revenue), 'Gold' (>= $10,000), or 'Standard,' usable both as a calculated column and referenced from report-level measures. Use VAR to avoid double evaluation, and explain why ALLEXCEPT rather than a plain CALCULATE filter is required for this to work correctly inside a calculated column.
questions.modelAnswer: The measure needs CALCULATE with ALLEXCEPT, not a bare SUM, because this expression lives inside row context (a calculated column, one row per customer) and must be converted into a filter scoped to that one customer before SUM(FactInternetSales[SalesAmount]) means anything company-wide-safe. Referencing CALCULATE inside row context triggers context transition: the current row (one CustomerKey) becomes a one-row filter on DimCustomer. ALLEXCEPT(DimCustomer, DimCustomer[CustomerKey]) then strips every other filter that might already be active on DimCustomer while deliberately preserving the one context transition just created on CustomerKey — so the SUM aggregates exactly that customer's full sales history, regardless of what other DimCustomer filters happen to be active elsewhere in the model at evaluation time. A plain CALCULATE(SUM(...), DimCustomer[CustomerKey] = EARLIER(...)) approach is fragile and non-idiomatic; ALLEXCEPT is the standard, maintainable pattern here. VAR computes CustomerRevenue once and reuses it across all three SWITCH branches instead of re-evaluating the same CALCULATE three times, which matters because this runs once per customer row — on a model with hundreds of thousands of customers, tripling that CALCULATE cost is a real, measurable performance hit, not a style nitpick.
questions.professionalAnswer: My approach here is: compute the number once, then branch on it. I wrap SUM in CALCULATE with ALLEXCEPT on CustomerKey, because this is going into a calculated column, which means I'm in row context — one customer at a time — and I need that row context converted into a filter scoped to just this customer before SUM means anything safe. ALLEXCEPT is what lets me say 'clear every other filter on this table, but keep the one tied to the current customer' — that's exactly the context-transition pattern. Then I stash that in a VAR and SWITCH on it three times instead of calling CALCULATE three separate times — on a customer table with real volume, that's not a style choice, it's cutting the evaluation cost by two-thirds. I'd also mention: if this needs to work as a report-level measure too, not just a calculated column, the same VAR/CALCULATE/ALLEXCEPT shape works fine either way, because CALCULATE's context-transition behavior triggers the same way whether the row context comes from a calculated column or from a measure being evaluated inside an iterator.
questions.example:
Customer Value Tier =
VAR CustomerRevenue =
    CALCULATE(
        SUM(FactInternetSales[SalesAmount]),
        ALLEXCEPT(DimCustomer, DimCustomer[CustomerKey])
    )
RETURN
    SWITCH(
        TRUE(),
        CustomerRevenue >= 50000, "Platinum",
        CustomerRevenue >= 10000, "Gold",
        "Standard"
    )
commonMistakes: Using a plain SUM with no CALCULATE, producing a grand total instead of a per-customer total
Using ALL(DimCustomer) instead of ALLEXCEPT, wiping out the context-transition filter entirely
Calling CALCULATE three separate times instead of once into a VAR
Forgetting that context transition only happens because CALCULATE is explicitly invoked inside row context
keyPoints: Calculated columns run in row context; CALCULATE inside row context triggers context transition
ALLEXCEPT preserves the context-transition filter while clearing other filters on the table
VAR avoids repeating an expensive CALCULATE across multiple SWITCH branches
SWITCH(TRUE(), ...) is the idiomatic tiered-threshold pattern

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces correct, working DAX using VAR and ALLEXCEPT
Correctly explains why ALLEXCEPT (not ALL or a bare filter) is required
Explains the context-transition mechanism accurately
Justifies VAR as a performance improvement, not just a style preference

questions.title: Build a dynamic RLS role with a bidirectional mapping table
questions.prompt: Design and write a dynamic RLS role for a model where a ManagerTerritoryMap table (ManagerUPN, TerritoryID) sits on the 'one' side of a relationship to DimSalesTerritory, which itself relates to FactInternetSales. A manager should see only sales for their assigned territory. Write the role expression, specify exactly which relationship setting needs to change and why, and state the one constraint that setting is subject to.
questions.modelAnswer: The role itself is a single dynamic filter on the mapping table: [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME(). The problem is relationship direction: by default an RLS filter only flows one way across a relationship regardless of the relationship's own cross-filter direction setting, and ManagerTerritoryMap sits on the side that needs the filter to flow outward — through DimSalesTerritory and on to FactInternetSales — not just filter itself. Left at the default, the filter on ManagerTerritoryMap would narrow that table down to the signed-in manager's row but never propagate out to actually restrict which FactInternetSales rows are visible. The fix is enabling 'Apply security filter in both directions' on the relationship between ManagerTerritoryMap and DimSalesTerritory, which lets the RLS filter — specifically, and only the RLS filter, not ordinary report filtering — flow in both directions across that relationship. The constraint to flag before enabling it: if DimSalesTerritory (or whichever table sits in the middle) already participates in more than one bidirectional relationship, this option can only be enabled on one of them — you can't bidirectionally-filter-for-security on two relationships touching the same table simultaneously. It's also worth validating with Test as role before trusting it, and testing for a real performance regression, since bidirectional security filtering has a genuine query-time cost on a large fact table like FactInternetSales.
questions.professionalAnswer: The role expression itself is simple — ManagerUPN equals USERPRINCIPALNAME() on the mapping table. The real work is getting the filter to actually reach FactInternetSales, because by default RLS filters are one-directional regardless of how the relationship's normal cross-filtering is configured. Since my mapping table sits upstream of DimSalesTerritory, I need to turn on 'Apply security filter in both directions' on that specific relationship — that's the one setting that lets the security filter, specifically, propagate the direction I need. The thing I always check before flipping that switch: does DimSalesTerritory already have another bidirectional relationship elsewhere in the model? Because if it does, I can only enable this option on one of them — Power BI won't let me stack it. After that, I validate with Test as role and I genuinely load-test it, because bidirectional security filtering isn't free — on a fact table this size it can show up as real query latency, and 'technically correct but three seconds slower' isn't a result I'd ship without flagging it first.
commonMistakes: Writing the role expression but leaving the relationship as single-directional, so the filter never reaches the fact table
Enabling bidirectional security filtering on every relationship touching the table instead of checking the one-per-table constraint
Not load-testing the performance cost before deploying
Confusing bidirectional security filtering with ordinary bidirectional cross-filtering (a different, unrelated setting)
keyPoints: Dynamic RLS role expression: [ManagerUPN] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()
RLS filters are single-directional by default regardless of relationship cross-filter mode
Apply security filter in both directions propagates the RLS filter specifically
A table can only have this setting enabled on one of its relationships if it has multiple bidirectional ones
Performance cost must be tested, especially on large fact tables

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct dynamic RLS role expression
Correctly identifies the need for bidirectional security filtering and why
States the one-relationship-per-table constraint accurately
Mentions validation (Test as role) and performance cost

questions.title: Build a Calculation Group for Time Intelligence Variants
questions.prompt: Your semantic model has a single base measure, [Total Sales]. Report authors keep copying the same YTD, prior-year, and year-over-year % logic into new explicit measures for every base measure in the model (Total Sales, Total Cost, Total Units), and the model now has 40+ near-duplicate measures. Build a calculation group named "Time Intelligence" with three calculation items (YTD, PY, YoY %) that work against ANY base measure dropped into a visual, without creating a single new explicit measure.
questions.modelAnswer: The fix is a calculation group, not more measures. Every calculation item's expression is built on SELECTEDMEASURE(), which is a placeholder that resolves to whatever measure is in the visual's values well at query time — that's what lets one group serve Total Sales, Total Cost, and Total Units without duplication. YTD wraps SELECTEDMEASURE() in CALCULATE with DATESYTD, which requires a contiguous, marked date table. PY uses SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, and YoY % computes both periods in variables and divides with DIVIDE() to avoid blowing up on a zero or missing prior year. Each calculation item also needs an Ordinal set so items display in YTD/PY/YoY order rather than alphabetically, and ideally a format string expression (SELECTEDMEASUREFORMATSTRING()) so YoY % renders as a percentage while the dollar items keep currency formatting. The group also needs a sensible Precedence value if other calculation groups exist in the model, since Power BI applies calculation groups in precedence order and a collision silently changes results.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by naming the real problem: this isn't a DAX problem, it's a measure-proliferation problem, and the fix is a calculation group in Tabular Editor or the model view. I'd create the group 'Time Intelligence' with three calculation items. For each item's expression I lean on SELECTEDMEASURE() instead of hard-coding [Total Sales], because that's the whole point — it lets the same calculation item apply to whichever base measure the report author drops into the matrix. For YTD I'd wrap that in CALCULATE(..., DATESYTD('Date'[Date])), for PY I'd swap in SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, and for YoY % I'd stash current and prior values in variables and divide with DIVIDE so a zero prior year returns blank instead of erroring. Then I'd set the Ordinal property on each item so they sort logically in the field list, and double check there isn't already a calculation group in the model that would collide on precedence — if there is, I'd set precedence explicitly rather than let Power BI pick.
commonMistakes: Hard-coding [Total Sales] inside the calculation item instead of SELECTEDMEASURE(), which defeats the whole purpose of the group
Using DATESYTD/SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR against a date column that isn't marked as the model's official date table or isn't contiguous
Computing YoY % with a plain division instead of DIVIDE(), causing errors or infinities when the prior period is zero or blank
Leaving calculation items in default alphabetical order instead of setting Ordinal, so YoY % shows before YTD in the field list
Forgetting to set a format-string expression, so YoY % renders as a raw decimal like 0.142 instead of 14.2%
Creating a second calculation group later without checking precedence, causing one group to silently override the other
keyPoints: Calculation items use SELECTEDMEASURE() so one group serves every base measure in the model
Time-intelligence functions like DATESYTD and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR require a contiguous, marked date table
DIVIDE() is used for YoY % to handle zero or blank prior-period values gracefully
Ordinal controls display order of calculation items in the field list
A format-string expression (SELECTEDMEASUREFORMATSTRING or a literal) gives YoY % its own percentage format independent of the dollar items
Precedence must be managed deliberately once more than one calculation group exists in the model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of SELECTEDMEASURE() instead of a hard-coded measure
Correct time-intelligence DAX (DATESYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR)
YoY % uses DIVIDE() to handle zero/blank prior period
Identifies marked contiguous date table requirement
Addresses ordinal/format string and precedence considerations

questions.title: Restore Query Folding Broken by a Custom Column
questions.prompt: A Power Query against an on-prem SQL Server source was folding cleanly (filters and column selection pushed down to SQL) until someone added a custom column using Text.Proper and a nested if/then/else on a text field. The view in Power Query Editor now shows the full multi-million-row table being pulled before any filtering happens client-side, and the scheduled refresh went from 6 minutes to 45. Rewrite the query so folding is preserved as long as possible, and explain where the unfoldable step should be placed if it truly cannot be avoided.
questions.code:
let
    Source = Sql.Database("sqlsrv01", "Sales"),
    dbo_Customers = Source{[Schema="dbo",Item="Customers"]}[Data],
    #"Added Custom" = Table.AddColumn(dbo_Customers, "CustomerTier", each if Text.Proper([Segment]) = "Enterprise" then "Tier 1" else "Tier 2"),
    #"Filtered Rows" = Table.SelectRows(#"Added Custom", each [Country] = "US")
in
    #"Filtered Rows"
questions.modelAnswer: Text.Proper is one of the M functions with no SQL translation, so the moment it appears, the M engine stops folding every step after it and pulls the entire table locally. The fix is to reorder: do every foldable operation — Table.SelectRows filtering, column selection, joins against other SQL tables — before the Text.Proper-based custom column, not after. In this case Segment is being proper-cased only to compare against a literal, so the better fix is to drop Text.Proper entirely and compare with Text.Upper or a case-insensitive comparer, both of which still may not fold either, but at minimum the Table.SelectRows on [Country]="US" should run first so SQL does the heavy filtering and only the already-small result set hits the unfoldable step. If an unfoldable transformation is unavoidable, it should be the last step in the query, and Table.Buffer can be added just before it only if the same buffered table is reused multiple times downstream — Table.Buffer does not restore folding, it only prevents re-evaluation of an already-local table.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd right-click the step before Added Custom and confirm 'View Native Query' is still available there — that tells me folding was fine up through dbo_Customers, and it breaks exactly where Text.Proper gets introduced, since that's a function the SQL connector can't translate. My fix is to reorder the steps so Table.SelectRows on Country happens immediately after the source, while it's still eligible to fold, and only build the CustomerTier column afterward on the much smaller filtered set. I'd also question whether Text.Proper is even needed — if it's just being used to normalize casing for a comparison, I can do that comparison with Text.Upper on both sides, which is still unfoldable but at least isn't adding a whole extra transformation to the output. Then I'd check 'View Native Query' again after the reorder to confirm the filter step folds, and treat the custom column as the deliberate last unfoldable step rather than something that silently kills folding for the rest of the query.
questions.example:
let
    Source = Sql.Database("sqlsrv01", "Sales"),
    dbo_Customers = Source{[Schema="dbo",Item="Customers"]}[Data],
    // Fold-friendly filter runs FIRST, while still eligible to push down to SQL
    #"Filtered Rows" = Table.SelectRows(dbo_Customers, each [Country] = "US"),
    // Unfoldable custom column now runs on the already-filtered, much smaller set
    #"Added Custom" = Table.AddColumn(#"Filtered Rows", "CustomerTier",
        each if Text.Upper([Segment]) = "ENTERPRISE" then "Tier 1" else "Tier 2")
in
    #"Added Custom"
commonMistakes: Adding custom columns with Text.Proper/Text.Combine before filters that would otherwise fold, breaking folding for everything downstream
Assuming Table.Buffer restores query folding — it does not, it only stops a local table from being recomputed multiple times
Never checking 'View Native Query' to confirm where folding actually breaks
Filtering on the client with Table.SelectRows after an unfoldable step instead of before it
Using Table.AddColumn with a row-by-row M function on the full raw table instead of the smallest possible filtered set
Not considering whether the transformation could be pushed into a SQL view instead of M
keyPoints: Text.Proper (and most Text.* functions) have no SQL equivalent and break query folding wherever they appear
Fold-eligible steps (filters, column selection, joins to other relational sources) should run before any unfoldable step
View Native Query in the Power Query Editor confirms exactly which step breaks folding
Table.Buffer prevents re-evaluation of a local table but does not restore folding
When an unfoldable transformation is unavoidable, it should be the last step, operating on the smallest possible row set

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies Text.Proper as the folding-breaking function
Reorders steps so foldable filtering happens before the unfoldable column
Correctly explains Table.Buffer does not restore folding
Mentions View Native Query as the diagnostic method
Working, corrected M code in example

questions.title: Calculate Customer Cohort First-Purchase Date with a FIXED LOD
questions.prompt: Using an Orders data source with [Customer ID], [Order ID], and [Order Date], build a calculated field that returns each customer's first-ever purchase date, independent of whatever date filter is applied to the view. Then build a second field that classifies every order row as "New" or "Returning" by comparing the order's date to that first-purchase date, so a dashboard filtered to Q1 2026 still correctly shows a customer's March order as "Returning" if their true first purchase was in 2024.
questions.modelAnswer: A FIXED LOD is required because a plain MIN([Order Date]) recalculates per view filter, which is exactly the bug this question is designed to catch — filter the dashboard to Q1 2026 and a naive MIN would report the customer's first purchase AS Q1 2026, making every order look new. { FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date]) } computes at the customer grain independent of the view's filters and dimension shelf, because FIXED LODs are evaluated before dimension filters are applied to the visualization (though context filters DO still affect them, since context filters run before FIXED LODs). The classification field then compares [Order Date] to [First Purchase Date]: equal means that order IS the first purchase (New), anything later is Returning. One subtlety worth calling out: if the Q1 2026 filter is applied as a normal dimension filter, the FIXED LOD still sees all historical orders and computes correctly; if it's promoted to a context filter, the FIXED result would be recalculated only across the filtered set, silently reintroducing the bug.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the trap first: if I just drop MIN([Order Date]) on the view, Tableau recomputes it against whatever rows survive the current filters, so filtering to Q1 2026 would make every customer's first-purchase look like it happened in Q1 2026 — that's wrong. So I reach for a FIXED LOD: { FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date]) }. FIXED computes at the Customer ID grain across the whole data source regardless of what's on the filter shelf, which is exactly the independence I need. Then for the New/Returning flag, I'd write a simple calc comparing [Order Date] to that FIXED result — if they're equal, this row IS the first purchase, so it's New, otherwise Returning. The one thing I'd flag to the team before shipping this: order of operations matters. Regular filters don't affect a FIXED LOD's result, but context filters do, because context filters are applied before FIXED LODs run. So if anyone later converts the date filter to a context filter to speed up a different part of the dashboard, this calculation silently breaks, and I'd leave a comment on the field saying exactly that.
commonMistakes: Using a plain MIN([Order Date]) on the view instead of a FIXED LOD, so the result changes as date filters change
Not realizing context filters are applied before FIXED LODs and can silently reintroduce the filter-dependency bug
Comparing dates with datetime precision mismatches (e.g. one field truncated to date, the other with a time component), so the equality check never matches
Using INCLUDE instead of FIXED, which keeps the per-customer grain dependent on whatever dimensions are on the view
Forgetting that EXCLUDE filters (quick filters set to 'exclude') behave like normal filters and don't affect FIXED, but 'Apply to context' does
keyPoints: FIXED LOD computes at the specified dimension grain independent of the view's dimension filters
Context filters are the one filter type that DOES affect a FIXED LOD's result, due to order of operations
The New/Returning flag is derived by comparing each row's date to the FIXED first-purchase date
INCLUDE/EXCLUDE would behave differently and are the wrong choice here since the result must be filter-independent
Date type/precision consistency between the two fields is required for the equality comparison to work

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct FIXED LOD syntax at the Customer ID grain
Correctly explains why a plain MIN() aggregation would fail here
Correct New/Returning classification logic
Identifies context filter interaction with FIXED LOD order of operations

questions.title: Configure a Filter Action and a URL Action to Drill from a Dashboard to an External Ticketing System
questions.prompt: A support-operations dashboard has an Orders-by-Region sheet and a detail sheet, 'Order Detail'. Clicking a region bar should filter Order Detail to that region, but must NOT also filter the Orders-by-Region sheet itself (no self-filtering loop), and the selection should clear automatically when the user hovers away. Separately, a row in Order Detail needs a right-click action that opens the company's external ticketing URL with the Order ID and Region embedded as query parameters. Specify the exact action configuration for both.
questions.modelAnswer: Two distinct Tableau dashboard actions are needed. First, a Filter Action: source sheet 'Orders by Region', target sheet 'Order Detail' only (excluding the source sheet from the target list is what prevents it from filtering itself), Run the action on Select, and Clearing the selection set to 'Show all values' — which is the setting that makes the filter clear automatically on hover-away/deselect rather than persisting until another mark is clicked. Second, a URL Action triggered on Menu (so it's a deliberate right-click, not an accidental hover or single-click), with the target URL built from field placeholders, e.g. https://support.example.com/tickets?order_id=<Order ID>&region=<Region>. Tableau substitutes the placeholders with the values from the clicked mark at runtime. It's worth validating URL encoding — Region values containing spaces (e.g. 'North America') need to be allowed to URL-encode automatically, which Tableau does by default for placeholder substitution, and confirming the ticketing system's URL actually accepts those parameter names before shipping.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build these as two separate actions from Dashboard > Actions. For the drill-down, I add a Filter Action with Orders by Region as the source sheet. The critical setting is the target sheet list — I only add Order Detail, deliberately leaving Orders by Region out of the target list, because if I left it in, clicking a bar would filter the chart I clicked on too, which creates that self-referencing loop where the chart changes under your cursor. I'd set 'Run action on' to Select, and for 'Clearing the selection will' I'd choose 'Show all values' rather than 'Keep filtered values' — that's what makes it reset automatically instead of sticking after the user moves on. For the ticketing link, that's a URL Action, and I'd set it to run on Menu specifically so it only fires from a deliberate right-click, not an accidental hover. For the URL itself I'd use the field placeholder syntax, something like https://support.example.com/tickets?order_id=<Order ID>&region=<Region>, and before calling it done I'd actually click through it once to confirm Tableau URL-encodes the Region value correctly and the ticketing system parses the parameters as expected.
questions.example:
Action 1 — Filter Action "Region Drill to Detail":
  Source sheet: Orders by Region
  Target sheet(s): Order Detail   (Orders by Region intentionally NOT selected as a target)
  Run action on: Select
  Target filters: Selected Fields -> Region
  Clearing the selection will: Show all values

Action 2 — URL Action "Open Support Ticket":
  Source sheet: Order Detail
  Run action on: Menu
  URL: https://support.example.com/tickets?order_id=<Order ID>&region=<Region>
commonMistakes: Leaving the source sheet in the filter action's target list, creating a self-filtering loop on the sheet that was clicked
Setting 'Clearing the selection will' to 'Keep filtered values', so the filter sticks after the user deselects instead of resetting
Running the URL action on Select or Hover instead of Menu, firing the external link on an accidental click
Hand-building the URL with static text instead of Tableau's <Field Name> placeholder syntax, so it doesn't update per mark
Not verifying the ticketing system accepts URL-encoded parameter values, causing a broken link for regions with spaces or special characters
keyPoints: Filter action's target sheet list must exclude the source sheet to prevent a self-filtering loop
"Clearing the selection will: Show all values" makes the filter reset automatically when deselected
URL action is set to run on Menu so it only triggers on a deliberate right-click
URL uses Tableau's field placeholder syntax so parameters update per clicked mark
URL encoding of parameter values (e.g. spaces in region names) should be verified before shipping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct filter action source/target configuration avoiding self-filtering
Correct 'clearing selection' setting for auto-reset behavior
URL action correctly set to run on Menu with field placeholders
Notes URL-encoding / parameter validation concern

questions.title: Write a Running 12-Month Total and Month-over-Month Delta for a BI Semantic View
questions.prompt: A reporting view, MonthlySales(StoreId, SalesMonth, SalesAmount), feeds a Power BI DirectQuery dashboard. The dashboard team wants two new columns computed in the view itself (to keep the model thin): a trailing 12-month rolling total per store, and the month-over-month dollar change per store. Write the T-SQL using window functions, partitioned correctly per store and ordered by month.
questions.modelAnswer: Both columns are windowed aggregates partitioned by StoreId and ordered by SalesMonth, but they need different frame/function choices. The rolling 12-month total uses SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) — ROWS BETWEEN, not RANGE, is deliberate: ROWS counts physical rows (12 monthly rows including the current one), while RANGE would group by value ties on SalesMonth, which isn't the intent here. The month-over-month delta uses LAG(SalesAmount, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth) to pull the prior month's value into the same row, then subtracts it from the current SalesAmount; the first month per store correctly returns NULL since there's no prior month to compare against, which is the right behavior rather than something to coalesce away. One real gotcha: if a store has a gap month with no row at all (zero sales recorded as a missing row rather than a zero row), the rolling total silently covers fewer than 12 calendar months and the MoM delta compares against the wrong month — that assumes one row exists per store per calendar month, which should be validated against the actual data before shipping this.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this as a single SELECT with two window functions, both partitioned by StoreId so one store's numbers never bleed into another's, and both ordered by SalesMonth since that's what 'trailing' and 'month-over-month' are relative to. For the rolling 12-month total, I'd use SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) — I'd specifically call out ROWS instead of RANGE, because ROWS gives me a fixed window of 12 physical rows, whereas RANGE would behave oddly if there were ever duplicate month values. For month-over-month, LAG is the natural fit: LAG(SalesAmount) OVER (PARTITION BY StoreId ORDER BY SalesMonth) grabs last month's value onto the current row so I can just subtract. I'd leave the first row per store as NULL rather than coalescing it to zero, since there genuinely isn't a prior month to compare against and that's a meaningful distinction for the dashboard. Before calling this done, I'd ask whether every store has exactly one row per calendar month with no gaps — if a month is just missing instead of zero, both the rolling total and the MoM comparison quietly go wrong, and that's worth checking against the real table before trusting the output.
questions.example:
SELECT
    StoreId,
    SalesMonth,
    SalesAmount,
    SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY StoreId
        ORDER BY SalesMonth
        ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS Rolling12MonthTotal,
    SalesAmount - LAG(SalesAmount, 1) OVER (
        PARTITION BY StoreId
        ORDER BY SalesMonth
    ) AS MonthOverMonthDelta
FROM MonthlySales
ORDER BY StoreId, SalesMonth;
commonMistakes: Using RANGE BETWEEN instead of ROWS BETWEEN for the rolling window, which behaves incorrectly with duplicate or tied order-by values
Omitting PARTITION BY StoreId, causing the rolling total and LAG to blend data across different stores
Coalescing the first-row NULL from LAG to zero, masking the fact that no prior month exists for comparison
Not validating that each store has exactly one row per calendar month, which silently breaks both the rolling total and the MoM delta if months are missing
Using a self-join or correlated subquery instead of window functions, which is far slower and harder to maintain
keyPoints: PARTITION BY StoreId keeps both window calculations scoped per store
ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives a fixed 12-row rolling window, distinct from RANGE semantics
LAG(SalesAmount, 1) retrieves the prior month's value for the month-over-month subtraction
The first row per store legitimately returns NULL for the MoM delta and should not be coalesced
Correctness depends on one row existing per store per calendar month with no gaps

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct PARTITION BY/ORDER BY on both window functions
Correct use of ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (not RANGE)
Correct LAG-based month-over-month delta calculation
Identifies the gap-month / missing-row data assumption risk

questions.title: Write a MERGE Statement for an Incremental Load into a Reporting Fact Table
questions.prompt: A nightly pipeline lands new and changed rows into a staging table, StagingOrders, keyed by OrderId, with a LastModifiedUtc watermark column. The target reporting table, FactOrders, must end up with exactly one row per OrderId: new orders inserted, changed orders updated in place (so DAX measures referencing FactOrders stay correct), and any staged row whose LastModifiedUtc is older than or equal to what's already in FactOrders ignored entirely. Write the MERGE statement.
questions.code:
CREATE TABLE FactOrders (
    OrderId INT PRIMARY KEY,
    CustomerId INT,
    OrderDate DATE,
    Status VARCHAR(20),
    TotalAmount DECIMAL(18,2),
    LastModifiedUtc DATETIME2
);

CREATE TABLE StagingOrders (
    OrderId INT,
    CustomerId INT,
    OrderDate DATE,
    Status VARCHAR(20),
    TotalAmount DECIMAL(18,2),
    LastModifiedUtc DATETIME2
);
questions.modelAnswer: MERGE joins FactOrders (target) to StagingOrders (source) on OrderId. The WHEN MATCHED clause must carry an additional AND condition comparing watermarks — WHEN MATCHED AND Source.LastModifiedUtc > Target.LastModifiedUtc — because without that guard, MERGE would blindly overwrite every matched row on every run, including rows where the staged version is actually stale or a duplicate replay of an already-applied change, which silently reintroduces old values and corrupts history-sensitive measures. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET handles brand-new OrderIds with a plain INSERT. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is intentionally omitted — adding it would DELETE every FactOrders row that didn't appear in today's staging batch, which is wrong for an incremental load where most historical orders simply aren't present in a given day's staging set. The statement should end with a semicolon, which MERGE requires in SQL Server, and in a real pipeline should run inside an explicit transaction with the staging table truncated immediately afterward so the next run starts clean.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set this up as a MERGE INTO FactOrders AS Target USING StagingOrders AS Source ON Target.OrderId = Source.OrderId. The part I'd be most careful about is the WHEN MATCHED branch — I wouldn't just update unconditionally on a match, because staging could replay an order that's already been applied, or even contain a slightly stale snapshot. So I'd add Source.LastModifiedUtc > Target.LastModifiedUtc as an extra AND condition on WHEN MATCHED, which is exactly the watermark guard the requirements are asking for — anything equal or older than what's already there just gets skipped. For brand-new orders, WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET does a straightforward INSERT. The thing I'd deliberately leave out is WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE — I would NOT add a DELETE branch there, because that branch fires for every FactOrders row that isn't in today's staging batch, which in an incremental load is basically the entire history table; adding it would wipe out everything except what landed today. After the MERGE runs I'd also plan to truncate StagingOrders so the next nightly run starts from a clean slate, and I'd wrap the whole thing in a transaction so a mid-run failure doesn't leave the fact table half-updated.
questions.example:
MERGE INTO FactOrders AS Target
USING StagingOrders AS Source
    ON Target.OrderId = Source.OrderId
WHEN MATCHED AND Source.LastModifiedUtc > Target.LastModifiedUtc THEN
    UPDATE SET
        Target.CustomerId      = Source.CustomerId,
        Target.OrderDate       = Source.OrderDate,
        Target.Status          = Source.Status,
        Target.TotalAmount     = Source.TotalAmount,
        Target.LastModifiedUtc = Source.LastModifiedUtc
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Status, TotalAmount, LastModifiedUtc)
    VALUES (Source.OrderId, Source.CustomerId, Source.OrderDate, Source.Status, Source.TotalAmount, Source.LastModifiedUtc);
commonMistakes: Updating on every WHEN MATCHED without a watermark guard, so a stale or replayed staging row overwrites a newer value already in the fact table
Adding a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE branch, which deletes every historical fact row not present in the current staging batch
Forgetting the trailing semicolon, which SQL Server requires after a MERGE statement
Not wrapping the MERGE in an explicit transaction, risking a partially-applied load on failure
Omitting LastModifiedUtc from the UPDATE SET list, so the watermark never advances and every future run re-updates the same row
keyPoints: WHEN MATCHED includes a watermark comparison (Source.LastModifiedUtc > Target.LastModifiedUtc) to skip stale/duplicate staged rows
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET handles new OrderIds with INSERT
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE is deliberately omitted to avoid deleting historical rows absent from today's staging batch
The UPDATE SET list includes LastModifiedUtc so the watermark advances correctly
MERGE statement is terminated with a semicolon, and should run inside a transaction with staging cleared afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct MERGE join condition on OrderId
WHEN MATCHED includes correct watermark guard condition
Correct WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET insert logic
Correctly omits/explains avoiding WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE delete
Syntactically valid MERGE statement (semicolon, correct clause order)

questions.title: Use a Python Script Step to Flag Statistical Outliers Before Loading into the Model
questions.prompt: Before a transactions table (TransactionId, StoreId, Amount) loads into the semantic model, the analytics team wants an IsOutlier flag added per store: true if Amount is more than 3 standard deviations from that store's mean Amount. The existing M query already produces a table called dataset (matching Power Query's Run Python Script convention). Write the Python script to add the column using pandas, keeping the computation grouped correctly per store.
questions.code:
# dataset columns: TransactionId (int), StoreId (int), Amount (float)
# Power Query 'Run Python Script' step injects the upstream table as the variable: dataset
questions.modelAnswer: Power BI's Run Python Script step requires the result to be assigned back to a variable the Python Script step can read (the dataset remains the only output table Power BI pulls back by convention), so the script computes a per-store mean and standard deviation with groupby and transform rather than a plain groupby().mean(), because transform broadcasts the aggregated value back to every original row without collapsing the table — a plain groupby would return one row per store, destroying the transaction grain the model needs. ddof should be set deliberately (pandas defaults std() to ddof=1, sample standard deviation, which is almost always the intended choice for this kind of outlier flagging rather than population std with ddof=0). The outlier test uses the absolute z-score, abs(Amount - store_mean) / store_std > 3, and the result is cast to bool. A store with only one transaction produces a std of NaN, which would make every comparison false via normal float comparison, so NaN is safely treated as 'not enough data to call it an outlier' rather than erroring, but it's worth flagging explicitly rather than relying on silent NaN behavior.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from the fact that Power BI's Python step reads whatever's in the dataset variable back as the output, so I keep that name and just add a column to it rather than building a new DataFrame from scratch. The core computation is a per-store z-score, so I can't just call dataset['Amount'].mean() — that's a single number across every store, which isn't what's being asked. Instead I'd use groupby('StoreId')['Amount'].transform('mean') and the matching transform('std'), because transform keeps the row count identical and just broadcasts each store's mean and std back onto every one of that store's rows, so I can do the z-score comparison row by row without a separate merge step. Then IsOutlier is just abs(Amount - store_mean) / store_std > 3. One edge case I'd call out explicitly: if a store only has one transaction, std comes back as NaN and the comparison naturally evaluates to False rather than throwing, so single-transaction stores never get flagged — which I think is the right default, but I'd say that out loud rather than let it pass silently.
questions.example:
import pandas as pd

store_mean = dataset.groupby('StoreId')['Amount'].transform('mean')
store_std = dataset.groupby('StoreId')['Amount'].transform('std')  # ddof=1 (sample std), pandas default

z_score = (dataset['Amount'] - store_mean) / store_std
dataset['IsOutlier'] = (z_score.abs() > 3).fillna(False)
commonMistakes: Using dataset['Amount'].mean() for a single global mean instead of grouping per StoreId, flagging outliers against the wrong baseline
Using groupby().mean() directly, which collapses the table to one row per store instead of preserving the transaction grain
Not using .transform(), forcing an extra manual merge back onto the original table
Forgetting that a store with one transaction produces std = NaN, and not handling the resulting NaN comparison explicitly
Renaming or replacing the dataset variable instead of adding the column to it, breaking Power Query's expected output contract
Using population standard deviation (ddof=0) without realizing pandas' default std() is already sample standard deviation (ddof=1), and not making that choice deliberately
keyPoints: Per-store mean/std computed with groupby('StoreId')[...].transform(), preserving the original row grain
z-score test uses absolute value and a threshold of 3 standard deviations
NaN std (single-transaction stores) is handled explicitly via fillna(False) rather than left to propagate silently
The output column is added directly onto the dataset variable, matching Power Query's Run Python Script convention
ddof (sample vs. population standard deviation) is a deliberate, stated choice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct per-store grouping using transform (not a collapsing groupby)
Correct z-score / outlier threshold logic
Handles NaN std for single-transaction stores explicitly
Respects Power Query's dataset variable convention
States ddof/sample-vs-population std choice deliberately

questions.title: Use LET and Dynamic Arrays to Rank and Flag Top Performers Without Helper Columns
questions.prompt: A sales leaderboard sheet has Rep (A2:A50) and Revenue (B2:B50), both dynamic ranges that grow weekly. Stakeholders want a single formula in one cell that spills a two-column array: each rep's rank by revenue (ties broken by giving the earlier row the better rank) and a text flag "Top 5" or "" next to it, without adding any helper columns to the sheet. Write the formula using LET and dynamic array functions.
questions.code: Named ranges: Reps = A2:A50 (dynamic, grows weekly), Revenue = B2:B50 (dynamic, grows weekly)
questions.modelAnswer: LET lets the formula name intermediate arrays once and reuse them, which both makes the formula readable and avoids recomputing RANK logic multiple times. The rank itself can't use plain RANK/RANK.EQ alone for tie-breaking by row order the way the requirement specifies, so the robust approach adds a tiny row-position tiebreaker: COUNTIF-style comparison via SUMPRODUCT, or more cleanly, RANK.EQ(Revenue,Revenue,0) combined with COUNTIFS of rows above with an equal value to bump later duplicates down — in practice this is expressed as rnk = RANK.EQ(Revenue,Revenue,0)+COUNTIFS(OFFSET(...)) or, more simply with dynamic arrays, a SUMPRODUCT-based rank: SUMPRODUCT((Revenue>Revenue_i))+1 adjusted with row index for ties. The flag array uses IF(rnk<=5, "Top 5", "") evaluated element-wise since dynamic arrays broadcast automatically. HSTACK combines the two single-column arrays into the required two-column spill, and because Reps/Revenue are already dynamic named ranges, the whole formula re-spills automatically as rows are added with no helper columns and no manual range edits.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this inside a single LET so I only compute the rank array once and can reference it twice — once for the rank column, once to derive the flag. For the rank itself, plain RANK.EQ would give true ties the same number, but the requirement wants earlier rows to win ties, so I'd compute a tiebreak nudge using the row's position — effectively RANK.EQ(Revenue, Revenue) and then subtract a tiny fraction based on ROW() for rows with equal revenue so earlier rows always resolve to the better rank without changing the displayed values meaningfully, or alternatively build the comparison directly with SUMPRODUCT comparing each value against all others plus a position tiebreak. Once I have that rank array as a LET variable, the flag is just IF(rank<=5,"Top 5","") — dynamic arrays apply that element-wise automatically, no fill-down needed. Then I'd use HSTACK to glue the rank array and the flag array together side by side into the two-column spill the stakeholders asked for. Because I built this off the Reps/Revenue named ranges which are already dynamic, adding a new rep next week just grows the spill automatically — no helper column, no formula re-entry.
questions.example:
=LET(
    rev, Revenue,
    n, ROWS(rev),
    rowPos, SEQUENCE(n),
    rnk, SUMPRODUCT_RANK := RANK.EQ(rev, rev, 0) + MAP(rowPos, LAMBDA(r,
        SUMPRODUCT((rev = INDEX(rev, r)) * (rowPos < r))
    )),
    flag, IF(rnk <= 5, "Top 5", ""),
    HSTACK(rnk, flag)
)
commonMistakes: Using plain RANK.EQ alone, which gives duplicate ranks on ties instead of the required earlier-row-wins tiebreak
Hard-coding the range size (e.g. A2:A50) instead of referencing the dynamic named range, breaking as new reps are added
Using VSTACK instead of HSTACK, producing a single stacked column instead of the required two-column side-by-side spill
Adding a helper column to pre-compute rank before flagging, which the requirement explicitly disallows
Not wrapping the logic in LET, forcing the rank expression to be recomputed separately for both the rank output and the flag output
keyPoints: LET names intermediate arrays once, avoiding duplicate computation of the rank logic
Tie-breaking favors the earlier row, not Excel's default equal-rank-on-tie behavior
Dynamic array functions broadcast the IF flag logic element-wise with no fill-down
HSTACK combines the rank and flag arrays into the required single two-column spill
Formula references dynamic named ranges so it re-spills automatically as rows are added

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct LET structure naming and reusing intermediate arrays
Rank logic correctly breaks ties in favor of earlier rows
Correct Top-5 flag logic applied element-wise
Correct use of HSTACK for the two-column spill with no helper columns

questions.title: Configure Git Mode and a CI/CD Publish Pipeline for a Data Factory Instance
questions.prompt: A Data Factory instance has been built entirely by clicking in the browser UX with no source control, and the team wants Dev/Test/Prod promotion with pull-request review before anything reaches Test or Prod. Describe the Git configuration needed in Data Factory itself, and write the key snippet of the Azure DevOps YAML pipeline step that deploys the generated ARM template into the Test Data Factory using parameter overrides (so the Test linked service points at Test resources, not Dev's).
questions.code:
Repo layout after Git integration:
  adf_publish branch (auto-generated, holds ARMTemplateForFactory.json + parameters file)
  main / feature branches (collaboration branches, hold the factory's actual resource JSON)
questions.modelAnswer: Data Factory's Git configuration is set under Manage > Git configuration, pointing the Dev factory at a collaboration branch (commonly main or a release branch) in Azure Repos or GitHub. Every change an author makes in the UX is saved to a feature branch and merged into the collaboration branch via pull request, which is what provides the required review gate — nothing reaches the collaboration branch without a PR. Clicking 'Publish' from the collaboration branch is what generates the ARM template and pushes it to the auto-created adf_publish branch; adf_publish is a build artifact, not something anyone edits by hand. The CI/CD pipeline then takes ARMTemplateForFactory.json from adf_publish and deploys it with an ARM/Bicep deployment task, overriding the environment-specific parameters (linked service connection strings, Key Vault references) defined in ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json so the same template deploys correctly to Test and then Prod without any hard-coded Dev values leaking through.
questions.professionalAnswer: First step, before any pipeline work, is wiring up Git configuration inside the Dev factory itself — under Manage > Git configuration, pointed at a collaboration branch like main. Once that's set, every change someone makes in the ADF UX lands on a feature branch, and getting it into main requires a pull request, which is exactly the review gate the team's asking for — nobody can push straight to the branch that matters. Publishing from that collaboration branch is what generates the ARM template into the auto-managed adf_publish branch; I'd explain that nobody should ever hand-edit adf_publish, it's purely generated output. For the actual promotion pipeline, I'd have the Azure DevOps YAML pull ARMTemplateForFactory.json from adf_publish and run an ARM deployment task against the Test factory's resource group, passing overrideParameters so things like the Test SQL linked service connection string get substituted in instead of whatever was baked in for Dev — the template itself stays identical across environments, only the parameter values change per stage.
questions.example:
# Azure DevOps YAML — deploy ADF ARM template into the Test Data Factory
- task: AzureResourceManagerTemplateDeployment@3
  displayName: 'Deploy ARM Template to Test Data Factory'
  inputs:
    deploymentScope: 'Resource Group'
    azureResourceManagerConnection: 'AzureServiceConnection-Test'
    subscriptionId: '$(testSubscriptionId)'
    action: 'Create Or Update Resource Group'
    resourceGroupName: '$(testResourceGroupName)'
    location: 'East US'
    templateLocation: 'Linked artifact'
    csmFile: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/adf_publish/ARMTemplateForFactory.json'
    csmParametersFile: '$(Pipeline.Workspace)/adf_publish/ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json'
    overrideParameters: >
      -factoryName "adf-test-bi"
      -AzureSqlDatabase_connectionString "$(TestSqlConnectionString)"
    deploymentMode: 'Incremental'
commonMistakes: Never configuring Git integration on the Dev factory, leaving all changes unversioned and unreviewable
Manually editing the adf_publish branch instead of treating it strictly as generated publish output
Deploying the same ARM template to Test without overriding environment-specific parameters, pointing Test at Dev's linked services
Using Incremental deployment mode assumptions incorrectly or switching to Complete mode, which can delete resources not present in the template
Allowing direct pushes to the collaboration branch instead of enforcing pull-request review via branch policy
keyPoints: Git configuration is set on the Dev factory, pointing at a collaboration branch with branch-policy-enforced PR review
adf_publish is auto-generated by Publish and should never be hand-edited
ARMTemplateForFactory.json plus its parameters file are the artifacts carried through the release pipeline
overrideParameters substitutes environment-specific values (connection strings, factory name) per stage
Incremental deployment mode is used so the deployment doesn't delete resources outside the template unexpectedly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes Git configuration and PR-gated collaboration branch workflow
Correctly explains adf_publish as generated, not hand-edited
Correct ARM deployment YAML task structure
Correct use of overrideParameters for environment-specific values

questions.title: Write a GitHub Actions Workflow That Validates a Power BI Project on Every Pull Request
questions.prompt: The BI team now stores semantic models as Power BI Projects (.pbip with TMDL) in a GitHub repo instead of binary .pbix files, specifically so changes are reviewable in pull requests. Write a GitHub Actions workflow that triggers only on pull requests targeting main, checks out the repo, runs a Python script (validate_tmdl.py, already in the repo) that fails the build if any measure's DAX expression is missing a description, and uses a repository secret for a Power BI service principal client secret needed later in the same job for a tabular model validation step.
questions.modelAnswer: The trigger block must be scoped with on.pull_request.branches: [main] rather than a generic push trigger, so the workflow only runs for PRs targeting main and doesn't fire on every commit to unrelated branches. actions/checkout@v4 is required before any script can see the repo's files. The Python step needs actions/setup-python to guarantee a consistent interpreter version rather than relying on whatever happens to be on the runner image, and the validation script's exit code is what fails the build — returning a non-zero exit code from validate_tmdl.py is what GitHub Actions interprets as a failed step, which is the actual mechanism that blocks the PR from being merged if branch protection requires this check to pass. The client secret must be referenced via ${{ secrets.POWERBI_SP_CLIENT_SECRET }} and passed as an environment variable to the step rather than printed or interpolated directly into a shell command string, since GitHub masks secret values in logs only when they come through env: or secrets context references, not when they're embedded in arbitrary strings that could be reconstructed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd scope the trigger tightly first: on: pull_request: branches: [main], so this only fires for PRs actually targeting main, not every push to a feature branch. First two steps in the job are actions/checkout@v4 to get the repo onto the runner, then actions/setup-python pinned to a specific version so the validation script behaves the same locally and in CI. Then I run the existing validate_tmdl.py — I wouldn't rewrite that logic, I'd just call it and trust its exit code; if it finds a measure with no description it exits non-zero, and that's what makes the GitHub Actions step itself show red, which is what branch protection rules key off of to block the merge. For the service principal secret needed by a later step in the same job, I'd pull it in via env: with the secrets.POWERBI_SP_CLIENT_SECRET context rather than concatenating it into a command string anywhere, specifically because GitHub's log-masking only reliably redacts secrets referenced that way — if it ends up inside a constructed string, it can leak into the logs unmasked.
questions.example:
name: Validate Power BI Project

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  validate-tmdl:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r scripts/requirements.txt

      - name: Validate TMDL measure descriptions
        run: python scripts/validate_tmdl.py

      - name: Validate tabular model (uses service principal)
        env:
          POWERBI_SP_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.POWERBI_SP_CLIENT_SECRET }}
        run: python scripts/validate_tabular_model.py
commonMistakes: Triggering on push instead of pull_request, so validation runs after merge instead of blocking the PR beforehand
Omitting branches: [main] from the pull_request trigger, running the workflow on PRs targeting unrelated branches
Not using actions/checkout, leaving the validation script with no files to read
Interpolating the secret directly into a run: command string instead of passing it through env:, risking an unmasked leak in logs
Ignoring the validation script's exit code by appending '|| true' or similar, which silently turns a failing check into a passing one
Hard-coding a specific runner's pre-installed Python version instead of pinning one explicitly with setup-python
keyPoints: Trigger is scoped to pull_request targeting main specifically, not push or an unscoped pull_request
actions/checkout and actions/setup-python precede the validation script
The validation script's non-zero exit code is the actual mechanism that fails the check and blocks merge under branch protection
The service principal secret is passed via env: referencing secrets.*, never interpolated into a command string
Workflow is written to run on every PR, matching the stated goal of reviewable semantic model changes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct pull_request trigger scoped to main
Correct checkout/setup-python steps before validation
Validation step correctly relies on script exit code to fail the build
Secret passed securely via env/secrets context, not interpolated into a string
Valid, well-structured YAML syntax

questions.title: Add Error Handling and a Child Flow to a Power BI Refresh-Failure Alert Flow
questions.prompt: A Power Automate flow is triggered by a Power BI 'dataset refresh failed' event, then calls a 'Post message in Teams' action. The team wants this hardened: if the Teams post itself fails, the flow should fall back to sending an email instead of just failing silently, and the actual alert-composition logic (building the message text from the trigger's dataset name and error detail) should live in a separate, reusable child flow rather than being duplicated inline. Describe the Configure Run After settings needed and write the expression used to extract the error message from the trigger output for the child flow's input.
questions.code:
Trigger: 'When a dataset refresh failed' outputs a JSON body including:
  { "datasetDisplayName": "Regional Sales", "error": { "message": "...", "code": "..." }, "startTime": "..." }
questions.modelAnswer: The composition logic (building the alert text from datasetDisplayName and error.message) is extracted into a child flow invoked with 'Run a Child Flow', which both avoids duplicating that logic anywhere it's needed and makes it independently testable. In the parent flow, the email fallback action must have its Configure Run After setting changed from the default (which only runs after the prior action succeeds) to explicitly include 'has failed' on the Teams-post action, because without that change the email step never executes at all when Teams fails — Power Automate skips subsequent actions whose predecessor failed unless Run After is reconfigured. The error-message expression needs coalesce() so a null error object (which can legitimately happen depending on the failure type) doesn't throw an expression evaluation error inside the flow itself: coalesce(triggerBody()?['error']?['message'], 'Unknown error'). The ?[] safe-navigation syntax is required throughout since triggerBody() properties aren't guaranteed to exist on every trigger payload shape.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pull the message-building logic out into its own child flow first, triggered by Power Automate's 'manually trigggered' / child flow type, taking the dataset name and error detail as explicit inputs and returning the composed alert text — that way if a third channel needs the same composed message later, it just calls the same child flow instead of someone copy-pasting the expression again. Back in the parent flow, the critical setting is on the email action: by default Power Automate only runs the next action if the previous one succeeded, so if I leave that as-is, a failed Teams post means the flow just stops and nobody gets notified at all. I'd right-click the email action, go to Configure Run After, and explicitly check 'has failed' on the Teams-post step so the email becomes the fallback path specifically when Teams fails. For pulling the error text out of the trigger body to pass into the child flow, I'd use coalesce(triggerBody()?['error']?['message'], 'Unknown error') — the safe-navigation question marks matter because I don't want a missing error object to throw an expression error inside the flow itself, and the coalesce gives a sane fallback string if it's genuinely absent.
questions.example:
Child flow: "Compose-RefreshFailureAlert" (trigger: child flow, inputs: datasetName (text), errorMessage (text))
  Output text: concat('Refresh failed for dataset: ', datasetName, '. Error: ', errorMessage)

Parent flow actions:
  1. Trigger: When a dataset refresh failed
  2. Run a Child Flow: Compose-RefreshFailureAlert
       datasetName  = triggerBody()?['datasetDisplayName']
       errorMessage = coalesce(triggerBody()?['error']?['message'], 'Unknown error')
  3. Post message in Teams (uses child flow's output)
  4. Send an email (V2)  -- Configure Run After: Teams-post step -> checked 'is successful' UNCHECKED, 'has failed' CHECKED
       Body: Child flow's composed alert text
commonMistakes: Leaving the email action's Run After on the default (runs only after success), so it never fires when the Teams post actually fails
Checking 'has failed' but forgetting to uncheck the default 'is successful' setting, which can cause unintended double-execution logic
Accessing triggerBody()['error']['message'] without the safe-navigation ?[] operator, throwing an expression error when the error object is absent
Dividing the error text out of the trigger payload without a coalesce() fallback, leaving the email blank or erroring when error details are missing
Duplicating the message-composition logic inline in multiple flows instead of extracting it into a reusable child flow
Forgetting that a child flow must be published and have 'Allow this trigger to run as child flow' type/permission set correctly before the parent can call it
keyPoints: Message-composition logic lives in a separate child flow, callable from any parent flow that needs it
Configure Run After on the fallback email action is explicitly set to trigger on 'has failed', not just default success
coalesce() provides a safe fallback when the trigger's error object is null or missing
Safe-navigation (?[]) syntax is used throughout when reading from triggerBody() since payload shape isn't guaranteed
The child flow takes explicit named inputs rather than reaching back into the parent trigger's context

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and configures Run After 'has failed' on the fallback action
Correct coalesce()-based expression for safely extracting the error message
Correctly extracts composition logic into a reusable child flow with explicit inputs
Uses safe-navigation syntax appropriately when reading trigger body
