questions.title: Nightly Load and Morning Reports Are Deadlocking Each Other
questions.prompt: The nightly ETL load now runs long enough to overlap with early-morning reporting queries, and you're seeing a spike in deadlock errors (1205) exactly in that overlap window. Write the query you'd use to capture the actual deadlock graphs (not just the error count), and describe the architectural fix once you've confirmed the access pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Server Profiler is deprecated, so I'd capture real deadlock graphs through Extended Events — either reading the always-on system_health session's xml_deadlock_report, or standing up a dedicated session — and extract the XML to see exactly which two statements and which objects/lock modes were involved. That turns 'we have deadlocks' into a concrete finding, like 'the ETL's bulk insert into FactOrderSales and a reporting SELECT doing a range scan are colliding on the same rows.' Once that's confirmed, I'd rank the fix options by durability: first, enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT so reporting SELECTs stop taking the shared locks that participate in the deadlock at all, which addresses it structurally rather than by luck of timing; second, shrink and restructure the ETL's transactions so they hold locks for the shortest possible time and touch narrower row ranges, through smaller batches or partition-aligned loads; third, if this keeps recurring, separate the workloads architecturally — widen or shift the load window, or move reporting onto a readable secondary — so the two workloads stop contending for the same locks on the same instance entirely. I'd recommend RCSI as the fast structural win and workload separation as the long-term answer if the overlap keeps growing.
questions.example:
-- Query system_health's ring buffer for recent deadlock graphs
SELECT
    xed.value('(event/@timestamp)[1]', 'datetime2') AS EventTime,
    xed.query('.') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file('system_health*.xel', NULL, NULL, NULL) AS f
CROSS APPLY (SELECT CAST(f.event_data AS XML) AS xed) AS d
WHERE xed.value('(event/@name)[1]', 'varchar(100)') = 'xml_deadlock_report'
ORDER BY EventTime DESC;
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't propose a fix off an error count alone — I want the actual deadlock graph first, so I'm pulling it from the system_health Extended Events session rather than reaching for Profiler, which is deprecated at this point. Once I can see exactly which two statements and which rows are colliding, I can say something specific, like 'the nightly bulk insert and a reporting range scan are fighting over the same rows,' instead of just 'we have deadlocks.' From there, my go-to structural fix is read-committed snapshot isolation, because it takes the reporting side out of the locking picture entirely instead of just making it less likely to collide. If the client's really pushing both workloads hard, I'd also talk about shrinking the ETL's transactions and, longer term, moving reporting to a readable secondary — but I'd never reach for NOLOCK as the answer here, because trading a deadlock for a dirty read isn't actually a fix.
commonMistakes: Tries to diagnose deadlocks from just the error count/frequency instead of capturing the actual graph
Jumps straight to NOLOCK on the reporting queries as a 'fix', reintroducing dirty-read risk
Only addresses the symptom (overlap timing) without checking whether RCSI would remove the lock conflict structurally
Recommends a replica without first confirming the deadlock is lock-contention, not resource-contention
keyPoints: Uses Extended Events (not deprecated Profiler) to capture real deadlock graphs
Translates the captured graph into a concrete statement-level root cause before proposing a fix
Evaluates RCSI as a structural fix for reader/writer lock conflicts
Considers transaction shrinkage and workload separation (replica) as complementary long-term fixes
Avoids NOLOCK as a quick-fix answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct approach to capturing real deadlock graph evidence
Correctly reasons from captured evidence to root cause
Proposes RCSI or equivalent structural fix with justification
Considers workload separation/transaction design as durable long-term fix

questions.title: A refresh schedule silently stopped running
questions.prompt: A finance semantic model's nightly refresh hasn't actually run in six days, but nobody noticed until a VP asked why the numbers looked stale. No one changed the schedule. Diagnose the most likely cause, explain why it happened silently, and design a monitoring fix so this specific failure mode can't go unnoticed again.
questions.modelAnswer: The leading suspect is the four-failures rule: Power BI automatically disables a scheduled refresh after four consecutive failures, with no warning beyond the failure emails themselves — and if those emails were going to an account nobody monitors, or had been removed from the semantic model's notification settings, the disablement would be completely silent to the team even though the mechanism itself worked exactly as designed. Something caused the first failure six-plus days ago (an outdated gateway, expired stored credentials, or a source schema change breaking a Processing Error: Type Mismatch) — within four attempts, the schedule turned itself off, and refresh simply stopped with no further failures to even generate more emails. The fix has two layers. First, root-cause the original failure using refresh history (status, duration, error per attempt) and confirm the gateway version and source schema haven't drifted. Second — more importantly for preventing a repeat — stop relying on a toggle anyone can silently lose track of: set up monitoring that doesn't depend on someone reading an email, such as a scheduled check (via admin APIs or a lightweight automated job) that alerts a shared channel or ticketing system whenever a model's refresh-enabled state flips to off, or whenever a model's last-successful-refresh timestamp exceeds its expected cadence. Relying purely on per-user failure emails is exactly the single point of failure that let this go unnoticed for six days.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess, before even opening refresh history, is the four-failures rule — Power BI will auto-disable a schedule after four failures in a row, and the only notice is a failure email, which is easy for an email filter or an inactive recipient to swallow completely. So I'd check refresh history first to find what the original failure actually was — gateway version, expired credentials, a schema change — fix that, then flip the schedule back on. But fixing today's incident isn't the real deliverable here; the real gap is that we had no way to know a refresh had silently turned itself off for six days. So I'd set up a monitoring check that doesn't depend on a human reading an email — something that polls refresh status or the model's refresh-enabled flag and posts to a channel the team actually watches the moment either one looks wrong. The failure-email mechanism did exactly what it was built to do; the actual bug here is organizational, not technical — we built a single point of failure around a notification nobody was reliably watching.
commonMistakes: Assuming someone must have manually disabled the schedule
Fixing the immediate failure cause without addressing why six days passed unnoticed
Relying solely on refresh-failure emails as the only monitoring mechanism going forward
Not checking refresh history to find the actual original failure cause
keyPoints: Four consecutive failures auto-disables a scheduled refresh with no further warning
Refresh history shows status/duration/error for every attempt — the starting point for root cause
Common original causes: outdated gateway, expired credentials, source schema change
The real fix is monitoring that doesn't rely on a human reading an email
Re-enabling requires fixing the root cause first, then manually flipping the schedule back on

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the four-failures rule as the likely mechanism
Uses refresh history to reason about the original root cause
Proposes a monitoring fix independent of per-user email
Distinguishes the immediate fix from the systemic one

questions.title: One gateway node offline breaks forty workspaces
questions.prompt: A single on-premises data gateway, installed in personal mode years ago on a departed employee's workstation, silently went offline over the weekend. Monday morning, scheduled refreshes fail across roughly 40 workspaces tenant-wide, and nobody can agree on why so much broke from one machine. Diagnose the architectural root cause and redesign the gateway setup so this can't happen again.
questions.modelAnswer: The root cause isn't really 'a machine went offline' — it's that a personal-mode gateway, which is explicitly single-user and non-shareable, somehow ended up as a load-bearing dependency for 40 workspaces across the tenant, almost certainly because semantic models across many teams were pointed at it opportunistically over time with nobody tracking that concentration. Personal mode exists for a solo learner or individual's own machine precisely because it isn't meant to be shared infrastructure — once it became exactly that, the organization had, unknowingly, built a single point of failure with no redundancy, no shared administration, and ownership tied to one person's workstation that nobody re-pointed when that person left. The fix is architectural, not a quick restart: migrate every semantic model currently depending on that personal-mode gateway onto a standard on-premises data gateway, which supports multiple users, multiple data sources, and — critically — can be clustered, with multiple gateway instances installed and registered under the same cluster name for high availability, so one machine going offline doesn't take down everything behind it. Gateway administration should move to a small group of named gateway admins (not a single individual's personal account), and semantic model owners should be audited and documented so 'which gateway does this depend on, and who owns it' is answerable without an incident. Going forward, gateway health should be monitored proactively — not discovered via a wave of Monday-morning refresh failures — and any new on-premises connection request should be evaluated against whether it belongs on the shared standard gateway cluster from day one, not bolted onto whatever machine happens to be convenient.
questions.professionalAnswer: The uncomfortable truth here is that the real root cause isn't the gateway going offline — gateways go offline — it's that a personal-mode gateway, which is explicitly not supposed to be shared, somehow became load-bearing infrastructure for 40 workspaces, and nobody noticed that creeping dependency until it broke. That's an architecture failure, not a one-time outage. My fix is to migrate everything off that personal-mode gateway onto a proper standard gateway, and specifically a clustered one — multiple instances registered under the same cluster name — so a single machine going offline is a non-event instead of a tenant-wide incident. I'd also fix the ownership gap: gateway administration needs to belong to a named team, not one person's workstation, and we need an actual inventory of which semantic models depend on which gateway, so this conversation next time takes five minutes instead of a morning of finger-pointing. And I'd put monitoring in front of gateway health going forward, because the way we found out about this — a wave of failed refreshes Monday morning — is the worst possible way to find out about it.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a one-time outage to restart rather than an architectural single point of failure
Not recognizing that personal-mode gateways are explicitly unsuited to being shared, load-bearing infrastructure
Migrating to a standard gateway without clustering it, leaving the same single-point-of-failure risk
No inventory of which semantic models depend on which gateway, making future incidents equally confusing
keyPoints: Personal-mode gateways are single-user and non-shareable by design — not meant for this load
Standard gateways support multiple users/sources and can be clustered for high availability
Ownership tied to one individual's machine is itself the governance failure
An inventory of model-to-gateway dependency prevents repeat confusion during incidents
Proactive gateway health monitoring beats discovering failure via a wave of refresh errors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the architectural root cause (personal-mode gateway as unintended shared infra)
Proposes a standard, clustered gateway redesign for HA
Addresses ownership/governance gap, not just the technical fix
Proposes proactive monitoring going forward

questions.title: Gateway Cluster Refreshes Succeed on One Node and Time Out on Another
questions.prompt: Your organization runs an on-premises data gateway cluster with three nodes for high availability. Scheduled refreshes against the same dataset intermittently time out, and you notice the failures correlate with which node happened to pick up the request. Diagnose the likely causes in a gateway cluster specifically (not a single-gateway setup), and describe the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A gateway cluster's whole value proposition is that any node can service any request, with the Power BI service load-balancing across whichever nodes are online -- which means the most common cause of node-specific failures is that the nodes aren't actually equivalent. The leading suspect is driver or component drift: if the three machines don't have identical versions of the data source drivers (an ODBC driver, an OLE DB provider, a specific connector version) a query that one node's driver handles fine can hang or error on another node with an older or mismatched driver version. Second: gateway cluster members need their recovery key and configuration kept in sync, and a node that was added later, patched separately, or restored from an older config can silently diverge from the others in ways that don't show up until it happens to pick up a request. Third: network path differences -- if the three gateway machines sit in different subnets, behind different firewall rules, or have different latency/routing to the actual data source, a node that can't reach the source as reliably will time out exactly as intermittently as this symptom describes, while the other two nodes succeed every time. Fourth: resource contention on one node specifically -- if the three machines aren't sized or loaded identically (one also running other workloads), that node can be the one that times out under load while the others handle the same request fine. The fix is to first identify which specific node correlates with the failures (gateway cluster logs identify which node serviced each request), then diagnose that node specifically against the other two: compare driver/component versions, compare network reachability to the source, and compare the node's resource utilization during the failure window. The durable fix is configuration parity enforced as policy -- identical driver versions, identical patch level, and ideally machines provisioned from the same image or a documented build checklist -- rather than treating each node as independently maintained.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that makes this a cluster-specific problem, not a generic gateway problem, is that it only fails on certain nodes -- which tells me the three machines aren't actually identical, even though the whole point of a cluster is that they're supposed to be interchangeable. My first move is to use the gateway logs to confirm exactly which node served each failed request, so I'm not guessing. Then I compare that node against the other two on the things that actually cause this symptom: are the data source drivers the exact same version everywhere, is there a network path or firewall difference that makes that specific machine slower or less reliable reaching the source, and is that machine running other workloads that are stealing resources the other two don't have to compete with. Once I know which of those it is, the immediate fix is usually straightforward -- patch the driver, fix the network rule, rebalance the load. But the fix I actually care about is the policy one: these three machines need to be provisioned identically and kept in lockstep, patch for patch, driver for driver, because 'it's a cluster' only holds up if every node genuinely behaves the same way, and right now it doesn't.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a generic gateway timeout problem without addressing why it's specific to certain nodes in a cluster
Doesn't check for driver/connector version drift across the cluster's member machines
Overlooks network path or firewall differences specific to one node
Doesn't use gateway logs to confirm which node served each failed request before diagnosing
Fixes the immediate symptom without proposing configuration-parity policy across cluster nodes
keyPoints: Recognizes that a gateway cluster's nodes must be configuration-equivalent, and failures suggest they aren't
Identifies driver/connector version drift as a leading cause
Considers network path/firewall differences specific to one node
Considers resource contention from unequal workloads across nodes
Proposes using gateway logs to confirm the failing node before diagnosing, and configuration-parity policy as the durable fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as a node-equivalence problem specific to clustering
Identifies driver/version drift as a leading cause
Identifies network/resource differences as plausible causes
Proposes a structured diagnosis using gateway logs and a durable configuration-parity fix

questions.title: Executive Dashboard Timing Out After a Premium Capacity Eviction
questions.prompt: Your team's P1 Premium capacity has run smoothly for months. This afternoon, users report the flagship executive dashboard is timing out, and its dataset's scheduled refresh just failed with a generic 'resource governing' error. The Capacity Metrics app shows a memory spike starting around 1pm, right after another team published a new self-service dataset to the same capacity. Walk through exactly how you'd diagnose and fix this as the BI Engineer who owns the capacity.
questions.modelAnswer: First confirm scope and timeline: open the Capacity Metrics app, filter to today, and overlay the Memory, CPU, and Overload/Eviction tiles against the 1pm spike. Eviction events specifically show which dataset(s) got unloaded from memory to protect the capacity — confirm whether it's the executive dataset itself or whether it's being starved by the new one. Drill into the new dataset: check its size, storage mode (Import vs DirectQuery), whether it uses incremental refresh, and its own refresh duration/memory footprint in the metrics app. If it's an oversized Import model refreshing on a tight schedule, that's the likely trigger pushing total memory over the capacity's limit and causing the executive dataset to be evicted and reloaded on every query (hence the timeouts). Immediate mitigation: pause or reschedule the new dataset's refresh, or move it to its own workspace/capacity if one is available, to relieve memory pressure now. Re-trigger the executive dataset's refresh once pressure drops and confirm it completes. Root cause: capacity-wide memory contention from an unisolated self-service publish, not a problem with the executive dataset's own design. Longer-term fix: workspace-to-capacity assignment review, autoscale or capacity sizing, and a memory-threshold alert so this is caught before users notice.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat this as a capacity incident, not a report bug, so I start in the Capacity Metrics app before touching the dashboard at all. I pull up today's view and line up Memory, CPU Resource Governing, and the Evictions table against 1pm — that eviction table is gold, it literally names the datasets that got unloaded under memory pressure. Once I see the executive dataset got evicted, I know the timeout is a side effect, not a model problem on that dataset. Next I go looking for what pushed memory over the edge, and the other team's new publish right at 1pm is too convenient to ignore — I check its size and refresh pattern in the same metrics app. If it's a big Import-mode model with no incremental refresh hammering the capacity on a schedule, that's my answer. I buy relief immediately — pause that dataset's refresh or move its workspace off this capacity — then kick the executive dataset's refresh again and watch it complete cleanly. Only after service is restored do I write it up: shared capacity with no workspace isolation and no memory alerting. I'd push for either dedicated capacity for tier-1 dashboards or alerting at 80% memory so I'm not finding out from angry Slack messages next time.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to optimizing the executive dataset's DAX or model before checking whether it was even the cause
Not checking the Capacity Metrics app's eviction/overload data and guessing from symptoms alone
Treating the refresh failure and the dashboard timeout as two unrelated issues instead of one capacity-level root cause
Restarting or refreshing the executive dataset repeatedly without first relieving the memory pressure, which just causes another eviction
Fixing the immediate incident but not addressing the lack of workspace/capacity isolation that allowed one team's publish to affect another's dashboard
Assuming capacity problems require buying more hardware instead of checking for an obvious single-dataset offender first
keyPoints: Uses the Capacity Metrics app's Memory/CPU/Eviction tiles to correlate the timeline before forming a hypothesis
Identifies that the new self-service dataset's publish/refresh is the likely trigger via its size, storage mode, and refresh cadence
Separates the symptom (timeout, refresh failure) from the root cause (shared-capacity memory contention)
Applies an immediate mitigation (pause/move the offending dataset) before re-attempting the failed refresh
Proposes a durable fix: workspace isolation, capacity sizing/autoscale, or alerting thresholds
Recognizes eviction as an expected Premium protection mechanism, not a bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses Capacity Metrics app data to establish root cause
Identifies memory contention from the new dataset as the trigger
Proposes correct immediate mitigation before long-term fix
Recommends sound long-term prevention (isolation/alerting/sizing)
Clear, ordered diagnostic narrative

questions.title: Dynamic RLS Shows the Wrong Data for One Regional Manager
questions.prompt: You've deployed a dataset with dynamic row-level security that filters sales data by region using USERPRINCIPALNAME() joined to a UserRegionMapping table. In Power BI Desktop, 'View As' with the manager's role works perfectly. But once published to the Power BI Service, one regional manager reports she sees ALL regions' data instead of just her own, while everyone else's RLS works fine. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: RLS bugs that only show up in the Service and not in Desktop 'View As' are almost always a UPN mismatch, because 'View As' tests under YOUR identity, not the actual user's — it can't prove what she sees. First I'd confirm in the Service itself; even 'Test as role' there isn't enough since that also runs as me. Instead I'd check Entra ID for her exact UserPrincipalName and compare it byte-for-byte against the value stored in UserRegionMapping. The classic culprits: trailing whitespace, a different casing or domain alias (e.g., jane.doe@contoso.com vs jane.doe@contoso.onmicrosoft.com), or her UPN changed after a recent rename/merger and the mapping table wasn't updated. If LOOKUPVALUE finds no match, it returns BLANK(), and a filter comparing Region = BLANK() can evaluate in a way that lets everything through rather than locking her out, meaning a bad mapping fails open instead of closed. I'd query the mapping table directly for her UPN, fix the row (or correct her UPN source), and republish. Going forward, I'd add a fallback so an unmatched user defaults to zero rows rather than all rows, so a bad mapping fails safe instead of failing open.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I rule out is 'View As Roles' in Desktop — that's testing my identity against the role logic, it was never going to catch a mismatch specific to her account, so I don't waste time there. I go straight to Entra ID and pull her exact UserPrincipalName, then open the UserRegionMapping table and look for her row character by character — this is almost always where it breaks, a stale UPN after a name change, an extra space from a copy-paste into the mapping table, or a domain suffix that doesn't match what USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns at runtime. What makes this one dangerous rather than just annoying is the failure mode: if LOOKUPVALUE can't find her UPN, it returns BLANK(), and depending on how the filter is written, comparing against BLANK() can let everything through instead of locking her out — so a bad mapping doesn't fail loud, it fails open and leaks data. Once I find her row is missing or wrong, I fix the mapping table and republish the dataset, then verify in the Service with her actual account or an equivalent admin test, not just View As. After the fix lands, I'd rewrite the DAX so an unmatched user gets zero rows, not every row, so the next broken mapping is a 'she can't see anything' ticket instead of a data leak.
commonMistakes: Relying on 'View As Role' in Desktop as proof the fix works, when it only ever tests the developer's own identity
Assuming the RLS DAX logic itself is broken when the actual bug is bad data in the mapping table
Not checking for whitespace, casing, or domain-suffix differences between Entra's UPN and the mapping table value
Not recognizing that LOOKUPVALUE returning BLANK() can cause the filter to fail open (show everything) rather than fail closed
Fixing just this one user's mapping row without auditing the table for other silent mismatches
Publishing a fix without verifying under the actual affected user's identity or an equivalent admin test
keyPoints: Recognizes 'View As Role' can't validate another user's identity-dependent RLS bug
Compares the user's actual Entra UPN against the mapping table value for mismatches
Identifies LOOKUPVALUE returning BLANK() as the mechanism that can cause RLS to fail open
Fixes the underlying mapping data, not just the DAX expression
Adds a safer fallback so future mapping gaps fail closed (no data) instead of open (all data)
Verifies the fix using the real affected user's context, not just Desktop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies UPN mismatch as root cause mechanism
Explains why 'View As' couldn't have caught this
Explains fail-open BLANK() behavior accurately
Provides correct fix plus safer fallback design
Verification approach uses real affected-user context

questions.title: Promoting to Production Silently Points the Report at the Test Database
questions.prompt: You used a Power BI deployment pipeline to promote a dataset and report from Test to Production. The promotion succeeded with no errors, but production users are now seeing stale, clearly wrong numbers. You suspect the Production stage is actually still querying the Test database. Walk through how you'd confirm this and fix it, plus how you'd prevent it from happening on the next promotion.
questions.modelAnswer: First confirm the hypothesis rather than assume it: open the Production stage dataset's settings and check data source credentials/parameters to see which server or database it's actually pointing at. Deployment pipelines promote the dataset's definition, but by default they don't know which connection string is 'Test' versus 'Prod' unless deployment rules are configured — without a rule, promotion can carry over the same parameter values used in Test, meaning Production silently queries Test data. Fix: configure deployment rules for the Production stage that explicitly override the data source parameter (e.g., a ServerName/DatabaseName parameter in Power Query) to point at the real production source, then re-promote or manually trigger a refresh with the corrected parameter. Verify by checking a few known production-only records appear and numbers match the source system. Prevention: deployment rules should be configured and documented for every stage before any pipeline is used for a dataset with environment-specific connections, and I'd add a post-promotion smoke test (e.g., a canary measure showing row count or max date) that's checked immediately after every promotion rather than relying on users to notice stale data.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't trust the 'promotion succeeded' message at all — pipelines can succeed while pointing at the wrong source, because success just means the artifact copied, not that the connection is correct. So step one is just going and looking: I open the Production stage, check the dataset's parameters or data source settings, and compare the server/database values against what Production is supposed to be. Nine times out of ten in this exact scenario, there's no deployment rule configured for that parameter, so promotion just carried the Test value forward unchanged — Power BI has no way to know Test and Prod should differ unless I tell it. Once I confirm that, the fix is mechanical: set up a deployment rule on the Production stage that pins the connection parameter to the real production server, then re-run the refresh with that corrected parameter and spot-check the numbers against the source system before telling anyone it's fixed. But the incident isn't closed until I fix the process, not just this one dataset — I go back and make sure every dataset with environment-specific connections on this pipeline has explicit deployment rules set, and I add a lightweight canary check, like a last-refreshed-date or row-count tile, that I glance at right after every future promotion instead of waiting for a user to notice the numbers look off.
commonMistakes: Trusting 'promotion succeeded' as proof the data source is correct, instead of directly inspecting the connection
Not knowing that deployment pipelines require explicit deployment rules to override environment-specific parameters between stages
Fixing the one dataset's connection without checking whether other datasets on the same pipeline have the same unconfigured-rule problem
Re-promoting repeatedly without first fixing the underlying missing deployment rule, which just reproduces the same bug
Not adding any post-promotion verification step, leaving the next promotion vulnerable to the same silent failure
Assuming this is a refresh problem and troubleshooting refresh schedules instead of the data source binding itself
keyPoints: Directly inspects the Production dataset's actual data source/parameter values rather than trusting pipeline success status
Correctly identifies missing deployment rules as the mechanism that let Test's connection carry into Production
Applies the fix via deployment rules, not a one-off manual edit that will be overwritten next promotion
Verifies the fix against real production data after correcting the parameter
Audits other datasets on the pipeline for the same gap
Adds a repeatable post-promotion verification step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses missing deployment rules as root cause
Verification method directly inspects data source rather than trusting pipeline UI
Fix uses deployment rules rather than a fragile manual workaround
Addresses other at-risk datasets, not just this one
Proposes concrete post-promotion verification process

questions.title: A Pandas Preprocessing Script Silently Breaks the Nightly Power BI Refresh
questions.prompt: A Python/Pandas script runs nightly to clean and reshape a vendor CSV before Power BI picks it up via a folder connector and refreshes. This morning's Power BI refresh failed with a column-not-found error on a field that has existed for months. The script's log shows it 'completed successfully.' Walk through how you'd diagnose what actually happened and fix it, including how you'd prevent silent script failures like this in the future.
questions.code:
# nightly_clean.py (simplified)
df = pd.read_csv(vendor_path)
df = df.rename(columns={'Cust_ID': 'CustomerID', 'Amt': 'Amount'})
df['Region'] = df['Region'].str.strip().str.title()
df.to_csv(output_path, index=False)
print('completed successfully')
questions.modelAnswer: A script that logs 'completed successfully' but produces output Power BI can't read means the script's success check is too shallow — it's checking that the process ran to completion, not that the output is correct. First, I'd open the actual output CSV from last night and diff its column headers against a known-good prior day's file. The classic cause here is upstream schema drift: the vendor renamed, removed, or reordered a source column (e.g., 'Region' became 'Region_Code' or the column was dropped entirely), so df['Region'] either raised a KeyError that got silently swallowed by a broad try/except, or more subtly, a rename/merge step produced a differently-named or missing column without erroring at all. I'd check the script for any bare except blocks that could mask a real exception while still printing success. Fix: correct the script to handle or explicitly fail on the schema change, re-run it against last night's source file, and manually trigger the Power BI refresh once the output is validated. Prevention: add explicit schema validation at the top of the script (assert expected columns exist, fail loudly if not), and make the success log conditional on that validation, not just 'reached the end of the script.'
questions.professionalAnswer: 'Completed successfully' from the script is not evidence to me — it's a claim, and this incident is exactly why. I go straight to the actual file the script wrote last night and open it next to a known-good older version, columns side by side. That's the fastest way to see whether the expected field is missing, renamed, or just empty. In this kind of pipeline, the usual story is the vendor changed something upstream — a column got renamed or dropped in their export — and the script either hit a KeyError that got caught by an overly broad except block and logged as success anyway, or it didn't error at all because a merge or rename quietly produced garbage instead of failing. I read through the script looking specifically for any try/except that could be eating a real failure, since that's almost always how a broken run gets reported as clean. Once I confirm the drifted column, I fix the script to match the new reality or, better, make it fail loudly instead of guessing when a column it depends on isn't there. I re-run it against the actual source file, eyeball the output columns myself before trusting it, and only then kick off the Power BI refresh. Going forward, I don't want 'reached the last line of the script' to count as success — I want an explicit assertion on expected columns and row counts before the log is allowed to say 'completed successfully.'
commonMistakes: Trusting the script's own 'completed successfully' log instead of inspecting the actual output file
Not comparing yesterday's output schema against a known-good prior version to spot the drift
Overlooking broad try/except blocks in the script that can swallow a real error and still log success
Fixing the column reference in Power Query/Power BI instead of fixing the actual broken upstream script
Not checking whether the vendor's source file itself changed before assuming the Python script has a bug
Deploying a patch without adding any validation to prevent the same silent-failure pattern next time
keyPoints: Treats 'completed successfully' as unverified and inspects the real output file directly
Diffs current output schema against a known-good baseline to isolate the drifted/missing column
Identifies a likely culprit such as a broad except block or silent rename/merge masking a real failure
Fixes the root cause in the script rather than patching around it in Power BI
Re-validates the corrected output before triggering a manual Power BI refresh
Adds explicit schema/row-count assertions so future failures are loud, not silent

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that success logging masked a real failure
Diagnostic method inspects actual output/schema rather than trusting logs
Identifies plausible root cause (schema drift / swallowed exception)
Fix addresses the script, not just the Power BI symptom
Prevention: adds explicit validation/fail-loud mechanism

questions.title: A User Says She Can't See a Dashboard Even Though She's Directly Granted Access
questions.prompt: A user reports she can't see a published dashboard on Tableau Server, even though you can see in the permissions dialog that she has an explicit 'Allow' for View on the workbook. She's also a member of a department group. Walk through how you'd diagnose and resolve this permissions issue.
questions.modelAnswer: In Tableau's permission model, Deny always wins over Allow, regardless of whether the Deny comes from a different rule and even if it's less specific than her direct Allow. So the first thing I'd check isn't her individual rule — it's every group she belongs to, at every level: the workbook's permissions, the project's permissions, and any parent project if nested. I'd look specifically for a Deny set at the group level for View or a related capability on this workbook or its project, since a single Deny from a group she belongs to will override her personal Allow. I'd also check if the project is 'Locked,' which prevents workbook-level permissions from being customized at all, meaning her explicit Allow on the workbook might be getting ignored entirely because the project's own rules are what actually apply. Fix: either remove or adjust the conflicting group Deny, move her out of the group causing it if appropriate, or if the project is locked, change permissions at the project level instead of the workbook. Verify by checking her effective permissions directly, not just the rules, using Tableau Server's effective-permissions view if available, or testing with her account.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to stop looking at her individual permission rule, because I already know the single rule that matters most here — Deny always beats Allow in Tableau, full stop, no matter how specific or recent the Allow is. So I go look at every group she's in, and I check permissions at both the workbook level and the project level, because a Deny set on a group she belongs to, even in the background somewhere, silently overrides the Allow she clearly has. I also check whether the project is locked, since a locked project enforces its own permission rules over the workbook's, which would mean her workbook-level Allow was never actually in play. Once I find the conflicting Deny — usually it's a department-wide group that got a blanket Deny for a different reason, like restricting an unrelated sensitive dashboard in the same project — I fix it at the right layer: either exclude her from that group's Deny scope, restructure the project so unrelated content isn't sharing the same lockdown, or move the dashboard to a project with permissions that actually reflect what should be visible. Before I call it fixed, I check her effective permissions directly or get her to confirm she can see it, because permission rules can look right on paper and still produce the wrong effective result.
commonMistakes: Only checking her individual 'Allow' rule and not looking for a conflicting Deny at the group or project level
Not knowing that Deny always overrides Allow in Tableau's permission model, regardless of specificity
Not checking whether the project is 'Locked,' which can make workbook-level permission edits irrelevant
Granting her another explicit Allow rule as a workaround instead of finding and fixing the actual conflicting Deny
Not verifying the fix using effective permissions or the user's actual experience, relying only on the rules screen looking correct
Assuming this is a licensing or site-role problem before checking permission rules
keyPoints: Knows and applies the rule that Deny overrides Allow in Tableau regardless of rule specificity
Checks all of the user's group memberships for a conflicting Deny, not just her individual rule
Checks whether the project is locked and enforcing its own permission set
Fixes the conflict at the correct layer (group, project, or workbook) rather than layering another Allow on top
Verifies using effective permissions or a real test of the user's access, not just the rules UI
Considers that the Deny may be scoped to protect unrelated content in the same project

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly applies the Deny-overrides-Allow rule to drive the diagnosis
Checks group memberships and project-lock status systematically
Fixes the conflict at the correct layer rather than a workaround
Verifies using effective permissions or real access test

questions.title: An LOD Calculation Starts Returning Wrong Totals After Adding One New Filter
questions.prompt: A workbook has a FIXED LOD expression computing each customer's lifetime total, used to classify customers into tiers. It worked correctly for months. Someone added a new date range quick filter to the dashboard for an unrelated request, and now the customer tier numbers are wrong — they change depending on the date range selected, even though the LOD expression doesn't reference the date field at all. Walk through how you'd diagnose and fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: The LOD expression not referencing the date field is exactly why this is confusing, but it's the classic FIXED LOD and filter-order bug: FIXED calculations are computed before ordinary dimension filters are applied, but context filters (and data source filters) are applied BEFORE the FIXED calculation runs, changing the data the LOD even sees. So I'd first check how the new date filter was added — if it was dropped on as a normal filter, it should execute after the FIXED expression and not affect it; but if it was added to Context (the gray pill), the underlying data gets filtered down before the LOD computes its FIXED total, which would explain totals changing with the date range despite the LOD never mentioning dates. I'd check the filter's position: Filters shelf vs. Context Filters vs. data source filter. Fix: if the date filter is in Context and was never meant to restrict the lifetime-total calc, remove it from Context (right-click, Remove from Context) so it behaves as a normal dimension filter applied after the FIXED computation. If the business actually needs the LOD to respect the date range, redesign it as a FIXED on [Customer ID],[Date] or an EXCLUDE/INCLUDE LOD that explicitly accounts for the date dimension instead of relying on filter-order side effects.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail that the LOD doesn't reference the date field at all is the tell, not a red herring — that's exactly the signature of the FIXED-and-context-filter order problem in Tableau. FIXED LODs compute their result before regular dimension filters touch the data, but context filters and data-source filters get applied first, before the LOD even runs its computation. So if that new date filter was dropped on as a context filter — the gray pill — it's silently shrinking the dataset the FIXED expression operates on, which moves the lifetime-total numbers around with the date range even though the formula text never changed and never mentions dates. I go check exactly where that filter landed: regular Filters shelf, Context Filters, or a data source filter, because each one interacts with the LOD differently. Once I confirm it's sitting in context, the fix depends on intent — if the date filter was only ever meant to control something else on the dashboard and shouldn't touch the lifetime-total calc, I just pull it out of context so it filters after the LOD like a normal dimension filter would. If there's a real requirement for the lifetime total to respect the selected date range, then the FIXED expression itself needs to be rewritten to include the date dimension explicitly, not left to accidentally inherit a filter-order side effect that happens to produce a plausible-looking but wrong number.
commonMistakes: Assuming the LOD formula itself must be broken because the numbers changed, without checking filter order first
Not distinguishing between a normal dimension filter, a context filter, and a data source filter and how each interacts with FIXED LODs differently
Not checking whether the new filter was added to Context (gray pill) as the actual mechanism
Rewriting the LOD expression as a guess-and-check fix without first confirming the filter-order root cause
Not asking what the actual business intent was (should the date filter affect lifetime total or not) before deciding on the fix
Removing the new filter entirely instead of understanding why it was added and finding a fix that preserves its intended purpose
keyPoints: Correctly explains the FIXED LOD vs. filter order rule: context/data-source filters apply before FIXED, dimension filters apply after
Investigates exactly where the new filter was placed (Filters shelf vs. Context vs. data source)
Connects the filter's position to why an LOD that never references the date field can still change with it
Determines business intent before choosing between removing context or redesigning the LOD
Proposes a correct fix: remove from context, or rewrite LOD to explicitly include the date dimension if needed
Verifies the fix produces stable totals across different filter selections where appropriate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains FIXED LOD vs. filter-order mechanism
Correctly diagnoses the new filter's placement as root cause
Fix choice reflects actual business intent, not a guess
Verification approach confirms stability across filter states

questions.title: A Sales Dashboard Shows Revenue Numbers That Are Nearly Double the Real Total
questions.prompt: A Power BI report built on a T-SQL view is showing total revenue that's roughly 1.8x what Finance confirms is correct in the source system, but only for orders that have more than one shipment. The view joins Orders to Shipments to get ship-date for a delivery-time metric, then aggregates Orders.Amount. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and fix, including the corrected query.
questions.code:
CREATE VIEW vw_OrderRevenue AS
SELECT o.OrderID, o.CustomerID, o.Amount, s.ShipDate
FROM Orders o
JOIN Shipments s ON s.OrderID = o.OrderID;

-- downstream aggregation
SELECT CustomerID, SUM(Amount) AS TotalRevenue
FROM vw_OrderRevenue
GROUP BY CustomerID;
questions.modelAnswer: Revenue being inflated specifically for multi-shipment orders, and by a ratio rather than a fixed amount, is the signature of a fan-out join: joining Orders to Shipments on OrderID returns one row per shipment, not one row per order, so an order with 3 shipments contributes Amount three times once the view is aggregated downstream. I'd confirm by running SELECT OrderID, COUNT(*) FROM vw_OrderRevenue GROUP BY OrderID HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 and comparing row counts against Shipments per order — matching counts confirm the duplication mechanism. The view is structurally wrong for this purpose: it's trying to carry a one-to-many relationship (orders to shipments) while also exposing a one-to-one fact (order amount), so any aggregation downstream double-counts. Fix: separate the concerns — aggregate Amount from Orders alone (one row per order) and compute ship-date/delivery metrics from Shipments separately, joining only where needed and at the right grain, e.g., using MIN(ShipDate) per order if only first-ship date matters. I'd rewrite the view so revenue aggregates come from an order-grain query, and ship-date logic comes from a shipment-grain subquery joined back only for display, not for the SUM(Amount).
questions.professionalAnswer: The pattern tells me almost everything before I even open the query — it's only wrong on multi-shipment orders, and it's wrong by a multiplier, not a flat offset. That's the fingerprint of a fan-out join: something joined one-to-many and then got summed without anyone accounting for the duplication. I confirm it in about thirty seconds with a quick count — group the view by OrderID, filter to count greater than one, and check whether that count matches each order's shipment count. It will, every time, in this kind of bug. Looking at the view, the mistake is clear: it's joining Orders to Shipments to grab a ship date, but Shipments is many rows per order, so the join itself duplicates every column from Orders, including Amount, once per shipment row — and then whatever's downstream just sums Amount across however many rows survived the join. The fix isn't a tweak to the WHERE clause, it's a grain problem — I separate the two questions the view is trying to answer at once. Revenue needs to come from Orders at order grain, full stop, no join to Shipments involved. Ship-date or delivery-time metrics need their own query at shipment grain, collapsed to one row per order first, before it ever touches a join with Orders. I rebuild the view as two clean pieces instead of one fused query, and I verify by re-running that same per-order row-count check and confirming it comes back to exactly one row per order.
questions.example:
-- Order-grain revenue (no fan-out)
SELECT o.CustomerID, SUM(o.Amount) AS TotalRevenue
FROM Orders o
GROUP BY o.CustomerID;

-- Separate shipment-grain delivery metric, collapsed to one row per order first
WITH FirstShip AS (
    SELECT OrderID, MIN(ShipDate) AS FirstShipDate
    FROM Shipments
    GROUP BY OrderID
)
SELECT o.OrderID, o.CustomerID, o.Amount, fs.FirstShipDate
FROM Orders o
LEFT JOIN FirstShip fs ON fs.OrderID = o.OrderID;
commonMistakes: Adding DISTINCT to the aggregation as a quick patch instead of fixing the join grain that caused duplication
Not verifying the fan-out with an actual row-count check before proposing a fix
Fixing it by filtering to 'only the first shipment row' with arbitrary logic instead of properly separating revenue and shipment-grain concerns
Assuming the source system (Finance's numbers) is wrong instead of the report's query
Not checking whether other metrics in the same view are also silently duplicated by the same join
Rewriting the join as a LEFT JOIN without addressing that multiple matching rows still cause duplication regardless of join type
keyPoints: Recognizes the symptom pattern (ratio-based overstatement limited to multi-row relationships) as a fan-out join signature
Confirms the hypothesis with a concrete row-count query before fixing anything
Correctly explains why joining Orders to Shipments duplicates Amount once per shipment row
Fixes the grain mismatch by separating order-grain revenue from shipment-grain delivery metrics
Avoids superficial patches like DISTINCT that don't address the underlying grain problem
Validates the fix by confirming one row per order in the corrected query

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies fan-out join as root cause mechanism
Confirms diagnosis with a concrete verification query
Corrected SQL properly separates grain instead of patching with DISTINCT
Explains why join type (INNER vs LEFT) alone doesn't fix duplication
Clear validation step confirming the fix

questions.title: A Report Query That Used to Run in 2 Seconds Now Takes Over a Minute
questions.prompt: A nightly report query filtering orders by date has gone from roughly 2 seconds to over a minute as the Orders table grew past 40 million rows. The WHERE clause uses a function on the indexed OrderDate column to normalize it before comparing. Nobody changed the query text or the index. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and provide the corrected query.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd pull the actual execution plan (not estimated) for the query and check whether it's doing an Index Seek or a Scan on OrderDate — on a 40M-row table, a scan where a seek should be possible is the key signal. The WHERE clause wraps the indexed column in CONVERT(date, OrderDate), and applying a function to the column itself makes the predicate non-SARGable: SQL Server can't use the index's sorted order to seek, because it would have to evaluate CONVERT() against every row's OrderDate before it even knows which rows match, forcing a full scan. This likely always technically had this issue, but it only became painfully visible once the table grew enough that scanning became expensive — small tables hide non-SARGable predicates because a full scan is cheap when there's little data. Fix: rewrite the predicate to leave the column bare and move the transformation to the literal side, using a range comparison instead of transforming OrderDate: WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-10-08' AND OrderDate < '2026-10-09'. This lets the optimizer seek directly against the OrderDate index. I'd confirm the fix by re-checking the execution plan for an Index Seek and comparing logical reads/duration before and after.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't start by looking at the index or assuming it got dropped or fragmented — I go get the actual execution plan first, because 'nothing changed' usually means the query had a latent problem the whole time that only became expensive once the table crossed some size. And sure enough, the plan shows a full scan on a 40-million-row table even though there's an index sitting right there on OrderDate. The WHERE clause is the giveaway: CONVERT(date, OrderDate) = '...' wraps the indexed column in a function, and the moment you do that, the optimizer can't use the index's sort order to seek — it has to convert every single row before it can compare anything, so a scan is the only option it has left. This bug was there on day one, it just didn't matter when the table was small enough that a full scan was basically free; growth is what exposed it, not a change to the query or index. The fix is just to stop touching the column and instead express the same filter as a range against the raw OrderDate value — greater than or equal to midnight on the target day, less than midnight the next day — so the predicate stays SARGable and the optimizer can seek straight to the right rows. I make the change, pull the plan again, confirm it's an Index Seek now, and compare logical reads before and after so I have real numbers to point to, not just 'it feels faster.'
commonMistakes: Assuming something must have changed (index dropped, stats stale) instead of checking whether the predicate was always non-SARGable
Not pulling the actual execution plan and instead guessing based on query text alone
Rebuilding or adding indexes without first fixing the function-wrapped predicate that prevents any index from being seek-able
Fixing it by wrapping the literal in the same function (CONVERT on both sides) instead of removing the function from the column side entirely
Not validating the fix by comparing before/after execution plans or logical reads
Blaming table growth alone as 'just needs more hardware' instead of identifying the specific non-SARGable predicate
keyPoints: Pulls the actual execution plan to confirm a scan where a seek should be possible
Correctly identifies the function-wrapped column as the SARGability problem
Explains why this was a latent issue exposed by growth rather than a new regression
Rewrites the predicate as a range comparison against the bare column instead of transforming the column
Confirms the fix via execution plan (Index Seek) and reads/duration comparison
Understands that the index itself was never the problem

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses actual execution plan to diagnose scan vs seek
Correctly identifies non-SARGable predicate as root cause
Corrected SQL properly rewrites as a bare-column range predicate
Validates fix with plan/read comparison

questions.title: A Data Factory Pipeline Feeding the BI Warehouse Starts Failing Every Run
questions.prompt: An Azure Data Factory pipeline that loads a staging table feeding your Power BI semantic model has failed every nightly run for the past three nights with a permissions error writing to the sink, a Data Lake container. No one changed the pipeline, and it had run successfully for months before that. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: A sink permissions error with an unchanged pipeline, failing consistently rather than intermittently, points to something changing in the identity or permission layer rather than the pipeline logic itself. First I'd check what identity the pipeline's linked service uses to authenticate to the Data Lake — if it's a managed identity, I'd check whether its role assignment (e.g., Storage Blob Data Contributor) on that container is still present, since role assignments can be removed during unrelated access reviews or security hardening passes. I'd also check whether the container itself was recreated or moved, which can silently drop previously granted RBAC on the new container even if the name looks the same. I'd check the Azure Activity Log around the time of the first failure for any role assignment deletions or storage account/container changes. Fix: if the managed identity's role assignment was removed, re-grant the correct RBAC role on the exact container. If the container was recreated, re-apply the role assignment to the new resource and verify the pipeline's sink path still matches. I'd confirm with a manual pipeline run before trusting the next schedule, and document the identity/permission dependency so future access reviews don't remove it blindly again.
questions.professionalAnswer: Three consecutive clean failures on an unchanged pipeline is a strong signal that it's not the pipeline that changed — it's something underneath it, specifically identity or permissions, since that's the exact layer the error is pointing at. I go check what the pipeline actually authenticates as against that Data Lake sink, usually a managed identity, and then go look at that identity's role assignments directly on the container in question rather than assuming they're still there. The two most common stories at this point are a role assignment getting swept up in an access review or security cleanup that didn't realize this pipeline depended on it, or the container itself got recreated — maybe through a lifecycle or cleanup process — which looks identical by name but is actually a new resource with no inherited permissions. I pull the Azure Activity Log around the first failure's timestamp specifically looking for role assignment or storage changes, because that tells me definitively which story is true instead of guessing. Once I find it — say the Contributor role got removed — I re-grant it on the exact container, confirm the pipeline's sink path still resolves to that same container, and run the pipeline manually once before letting it go back on schedule. I don't stop there, though: I write down that this pipeline depends on that specific role assignment, so the next access review or storage cleanup doesn't blindly repeat this.
commonMistakes: Assuming the pipeline's code/activities broke when a consistent permissions error points elsewhere
Not checking the Azure Activity Log for role assignment or resource changes around the failure's start time
Re-running the pipeline repeatedly without investigating why the permission error is occurring
Not checking whether the sink container itself was recreated/moved rather than just losing a role assignment
Granting overly broad permissions (e.g., Owner) as a quick fix instead of the specific least-privilege role that was actually missing
Not documenting the dependency, leaving the pipeline vulnerable to the exact same removal in a future access review
keyPoints: Recognizes a consistent (not intermittent) sink permissions error as an identity/RBAC issue, not a pipeline logic bug
Investigates the pipeline's authentication identity (managed identity) and its role assignment on the exact sink resource
Uses Azure Activity Log to pinpoint when and what permission/resource change occurred
Considers container recreation/move as an alternative to a simple role removal
Applies a least-privilege fix and verifies with a manual run before trusting the schedule
Documents the dependency to prevent recurrence from future access reviews

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the issue as identity/RBAC rather than pipeline logic
Investigates managed identity role assignment on the specific sink resource
Uses Activity Log or equivalent to pinpoint the triggering change
Applies correct least-privilege fix and verifies with manual run
Documents dependency to prevent recurrence

questions.title: A CI/CD Pipeline Deploys a Power BI Report Change to the Wrong Workspace
questions.prompt: Your team uses a Git-based CI/CD pipeline to deploy Power BI report/dataset changes on merge to main. After a routine merge, the deploy step reported success, but the change actually landed in the QA workspace instead of Production, and nobody noticed until a stakeholder asked why Production still showed old numbers two days later. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and fix, including how you'd prevent this from going unnoticed again.
questions.modelAnswer: A 'successful' deploy landing in the wrong workspace means the pipeline executed correctly against incorrect configuration, not that it failed — so I'd start by reviewing the CI/CD job's logs for exactly which workspace ID or environment variable it targeted during that run. The likely cause is an environment variable (e.g., a workspace-ID variable) that's scoped incorrectly — either the production environment's variable wasn't set or updated after a workspace change, or the pipeline's branch-to-environment mapping pointed main at the QA workspace ID by mistake, possibly from a copy-paste error in the pipeline config. I'd check the pipeline definition's environment/variable group configuration for main's target and compare the workspace ID used against the actual Production workspace ID in Power BI admin. Fix: correct the environment variable/mapping so main truly resolves to the Production workspace ID, then manually trigger a redeploy to Production and verify the dataset/report updated with current data. Prevention: add a post-deploy verification step in the pipeline itself — an API call confirming the target workspace ID matches an expected value before deploy, and/or a smoke test checking a known data point in the deployed destination — plus require explicit review of the workspace ID as a reviewed line in any pipeline config change, since 'deploy succeeded' alone is not sufficient evidence of correctness.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fact that it reported success is almost the whole problem here — a pipeline can run a flawless deploy to entirely the wrong place and declare victory, because 'succeeded' just means the API call didn't error, not that it targeted what I meant it to target. So I go to the pipeline run logs for that specific merge and find exactly which workspace ID it pushed to. In this pattern, it's almost always a configuration issue, not a code issue: either the Production environment's workspace-ID variable wasn't updated after some earlier workspace change, or the branch-to-environment mapping in the pipeline config has main resolving to the wrong ID, maybe from a copy-paste mistake when someone set up a new environment. I pull up the pipeline's environment/variable group config and just directly compare the workspace ID it used against the real Production workspace ID in the Power BI admin portal — that comparison alone usually finds it in under a minute. I fix the mapping, redeploy manually to the correct workspace, and verify the actual report shows current data, not just that the API returned a success status. But the part I care about more is the two days nobody noticed — that's a monitoring gap, not just a config bug. I add a post-deploy check into the pipeline itself: confirm the workspace ID it just deployed to matches an expected constant, and ideally a quick smoke check against a known value in the destination, so a misdirected deploy fails the build loudly instead of quietly succeeding into the wrong place.
commonMistakes: Treating 'deploy succeeded' in the CI/CD logs as proof the deploy was correct, instead of checking which target it actually hit
Not comparing the workspace ID the pipeline used against the real Production workspace ID in Power BI admin
Fixing the immediate deployment without checking whether the branch-to-environment mapping itself is wrong for other pipelines too
Manually redeploying without first correcting the underlying variable/mapping, meaning the next merge repeats the same mistake
Not adding any post-deploy verification, leaving the next misconfiguration to go unnoticed for days again
Blaming the developer who merged the change instead of the pipeline's configuration and lack of safeguards
keyPoints: Recognizes that pipeline 'success' only confirms execution, not correct targeting
Investigates the pipeline logs/config to find the actual workspace ID/environment used
Correctly identifies environment variable/branch mapping misconfiguration as the likely root cause
Fixes the underlying configuration before redeploying, not just the one-off symptom
Verifies the corrected deploy against real Production data, not just a success status
Adds a post-deploy verification/smoke-test step to catch future misdirected deploys quickly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Recognizes 'success' doesn't confirm correct target and investigates accordingly
Correctly identifies environment variable/mapping misconfiguration
Fixes root configuration before redeploying
Verifies fix against real production data/state
Proposes concrete post-deploy verification to catch future issues faster

questions.title: A Power Automate Flow That Emails a Broken-Refresh Alert Never Fires
questions.prompt: A Power Automate flow is supposed to email the BI team whenever a Power BI dataset refresh fails, using a 'When a dataset refresh completes' trigger followed by a condition and a Send Email action. A refresh failed last night, but no alert email arrived, and the flow's run history for that time shows no failed run at all — it simply didn't trigger an alert path. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: If the run history shows the flow didn't produce an alert at all, rather than showing a failed run, I'd first check whether the flow even ran last night — if there's no run instance for that time, the trigger itself never fired, which points to either the dataset not matching the trigger's configured dataset/workspace, or a connection/authentication issue with the Power BI trigger connector. If a run DID occur but no email was sent, I'd open that specific run's details and check the condition step's evaluated inputs — 'When a dataset refresh completes' can trigger on success too, so the condition checking for failure status needs to correctly reference the trigger's status output. I'd check whether the status field name or expected value changed, or whether the condition has a logic error that never evaluates true for failures. I'd also check whether 'Configure run after' was set on the Send Email action to only run after the condition's 'is true' branch succeeds, and not on 'has failed/skipped,' since a flow can complete overall while silently skipping the alert branch if a dependency step failed and nothing was configured to run after that failure. Fix: correct the condition logic and/or Configure Run After settings, then force a test failure (or replay a historic failed run's data) to confirm the email actually sends before trusting it again.
questions.professionalAnswer: No failed run showing in the history is actually the most useful fact here — it tells me this isn't a flow-execution bug, it's either a trigger problem or a silent branch-skip problem, and I need to find out which before I touch anything. First I check whether the flow ran at all at the relevant time; if there's genuinely no run instance, the trigger itself didn't fire, and I'd look at the trigger's dataset/workspace scoping and its connection health, since an expired connection can make a trigger quietly stop firing without raising an obvious error. If a run did happen, I open it and walk the condition step specifically, checking exactly what status value it received from the refresh-completed trigger and whether the condition's comparison actually matches a failure state — this trigger fires on completion generally, not just failure, so a lazy or wrong condition can let failures through without ever going down the alert branch. I also check Configure Run After on the Send Email action, because if it's only set to run after the condition step succeeds, and some earlier step in that run failed or got skipped for an unrelated reason, the overall flow can report as completed while the email branch never executes — that's a classic silent-skip, and it's exactly the kind of thing that doesn't show up as 'failed' anywhere. Once I find which of these it is, I fix the condition logic or the Run After configuration, and then I don't just trust it — I force a test run against a known failed-refresh scenario and confirm the email actually lands before I close this out.
commonMistakes: Assuming the flow is broken without first checking whether it even ran/triggered at all that night
Not checking the condition step's actual evaluated inputs for that specific run, and instead assuming the logic 'looks right'
Not knowing that 'When a dataset refresh completes' fires on success and failure alike, requiring a correct condition to isolate failures
Not checking 'Configure Run After' settings on downstream actions, missing that a flow can complete overall while silently skipping a branch
Fixing the condition logic without testing against an actual failure scenario to confirm the email now sends
Treating 'no failed run in history' as evidence nothing is wrong instead of as a diagnostic clue pointing at trigger or branch-skip issues
keyPoints: Uses the absence of a failed run as a diagnostic clue pointing to trigger failure or silent branch-skip, not proof nothing is wrong
Checks whether the trigger fired at all and investigates connection/scoping issues if it didn't
Inspects the condition step's actual evaluated status value for a run that did occur
Understands the refresh-completed trigger fires on success and failure, requiring correct condition logic to isolate failures
Checks 'Configure Run After' settings for silent branch-skipping behavior
Validates the fix against an actual failure scenario before trusting the alert going forward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly treats missing failed-run history as a diagnostic clue, not evidence of no problem
Investigates trigger firing/connection health appropriately
Correctly identifies condition logic or status-matching issue
Identifies Configure Run After as a possible silent-skip mechanism
Validates fix against a real failure scenario
